^RECOGNITION OF NATIONALIST CHINA, MONGOLIA AND RED CHINA
Question No. 58*-Mr. Pigeon:
1.	On what date did the Canadian government recognize the government of nationalist China (Formosa) ?
2.	On what date did the Canadian government recognize the communist regime of Mongolia?
3.	Does the government intend to recognize the communist regime of China and, if so, when does it propose to do this and, if not, for what reasons?
4.	When will the government appoint an ambassador to Formosa?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to that question is as follows:
1.	Canada recognized the government of nationalist China on December 20, 1928.
2.	We informed Mongolia of our diplomatic recognition on January 27, 1964, through a normal exchange of communications with the representative of that country in a capital where he is accredited. A similar procedure had been adopted by the previous government in the case of Albania in 1959.
3.	The government does not intend, at this time, to make any change in Canada's policy toward China. The question of recognizing the government of Peking involves various

factors which must be weighed carefully: Canada's role within international control commissions in Indochina and the stability of the situation in southeast Asia; then, the future of the inhabitants of Formosa; finally, the possible repercussions at the United Nations. Forecasting the future is now precluded by the rapid evolution of the situation.
Nevertheless, the government maintains that a country as important as continental China cannot and should not be isolated from the flows of international exchanges. That is why it shall continue the policy that has been followed these past few years, that is to increase as much as possible our trade and cultural exchanges with communist China.
4.	The government is not contemplating the appointment of an ambassador to Taipeh.

subtopic: FRENCH CANADIANS
FRENCH CANADIANS
speechtext: How many French Canadian officials of the Department of External Affairs have left that department since April 23, 1963?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FRENCH CANADIANS
speechtext:
Since April 23, 1963, five French Canadian diplomatic agents left the Department of External Affairs. One was named general commissioner for the Montreal world exhibition, another one was appointed assistant deputy minister in the Department of Transport. Four other French Canadian diplomatic agents obtained leave without pay, one having been appointed director of the national economic council, and two others having assumed duties in the World Exhibition Corporation. These transfers from the Department of External Affairs to the World Exhibition Corporation show the direct relations existing between these two bodies.
At the administrative level, 29 employees (archivists, stenographers, messengers, etc.) left the department during that period; 10 of them were transferred to other services of the federal government.
Altogether, of the 110 persons who left the department during that period, 38 were French Canadians, which represents a proportion higher than that of the previous year, but equal to that of 1961-62.

1. Expenditures on projects submitted by the provinces and supported under the national health grants relating to research into the effects of water fluoridation and the effects of topical application of fluorides to the teeth total approximately $51,400.
So far as intramural research is concerned, in view of the fact that personnel of the Department of National Health and Welfare from three divisions and one directorate have been engaged intermittently over a period of 16 years on research into the effects of fluoridation, including topical fluorides, while at the
same time working on other programs, it is not possible to segregate expenditures on this project.
2. It is an established fact, from very extensive research, that the adjustment of the fluoride content of a water supply, whereby there is a concentration of one part fluoride to one million parts of water, brings about an average reduction of 60 per cent in the prev-valence of tooth decay to children consuming fluoridated water since birth. No ill effects have been noted.
This improvement in dental health of children, who will later be adults, ensures an improvement in general health, dental health being an integral part of total health.
3	and 4. The activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare in relation to fluoridation have from the beginning been limited to research, the publication of research findings and the provision of technical advice and information. No advice has been given for the specific purpose of influencing policy decisions.
However fluoridation of communal water supplies is of broad public interest and is considered to be of great importance in the total health picture of the population of Canada. As of November 1963 more than 3,800,000 people, or 20 per cent of the population, in 188 communities were consuming mechanically fluoridated water.
In addition to the 20 per cent of the Canadian population who are consuming water with fluoride content adjusted to one part per million, many thousands of people have been consuming for a lifetime, and even for generations, water which has been fluoridated from underground deposits of fluoride. No ill-effects have been observed.

subtopic: PROGRAM "THE OPEN GRAVE"-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of moving the adjournment of the house, pursuant to standing order 26, to discuss a matter of public urgent concern and importance, namely the outraged religious feelings of Christians of all persuasions and faiths across Canada concerning the television show "The Open Grave", to which reference was made a moment ago in the answer given to question No. 403.
I may say that to my recollection this is the first time I have moved such a motion. According to the answer given, it is to be shown by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation later this week, during holy week, the most sacred and solemn of the Christian year. Irrespective of the answer given to the question, advance information indicates that the showing will be a flagrant, scandalous and sacrilegious insult to a majority of Canadians. I say this because clergymen and outstanding religious leaders in both the Protestant and Roman Catholic churches have so commented.
As one who believes in freedom of speech, freedom of religion and the need for the C.B.C. to be an independent body, I cannot refrain from saying that we as Christians may question whether we include in freedom a licence to malign or hold religious faith up

to contempt. I say this because the C.B.C. is a public institution maintained by the people of Canada. While I have no personal knowledge of the facts connected with it, press reports indicate the show will cost Canada $50,000. That was on the radio this morning, so it must be correct.
I again emphasize this fact, that many leading clergymen of our country are deeply concerned over this particular matter. Therefore I say no more, except that this deserves to be considered by the House of Commons. Believing in freedom, it is our responsibility to ensure freedom as the portion of all our people.

subtopic: PROGRAM "THE OPEN GRAVE"-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Order, please. I have to determine whether there is sound and sufficient ground to adjourn the business of the house under standing order 26. As to the importance of the matter discussed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, there can be little doubt as to the general interest either for or against, but the criterion on which I have to decide this question is one that has been mentioned several times by previous speakers, namely, is there opportunity to debate this matter in an effective way?
The matter is urgent, important, and certainly of general public interest, but it does seem to me, when we are in a budget debate and when interim supply will be reached on Wednesday, that this whole matter takes on more the appearance of a grievance than of being of sufficient national urgency and importance to adjourn all the proceedings of the house at this time to carry on debate on the proposed motion. Therefore, in view of the fact that opportunity will be given this afternoon in the budget debate and in view of the fact that interim supply, I assume, will be considered by the house on Wednesday next, it seems to me there is opportunity to discuss this important matter.
In the circumstances I regret I do not think that the house should be adjourned under standing order 26.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Is the Prime Minister in a position to say when the Canadian troops in Cyprus will begin to carry out their duties as designated by the secretary general?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, the Canadian contingent of the United Nations peace force is in Cyprus at the present time and is carrying out certain duties. My colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in Geneva at the moment, where he has been discussing with the secretary general of the United Nations questions in connection with the authority which is required by that force so that it may carry out its peace keeping duties effectively. In these discussions the Secretary of State for External Affairs has gone over the whole matter with the secretary general. He is meeting U Thant again today and will be back in the house very shortly, at which time he will be in a position to make a full report to the house on this very difficult and very delicate matter.
In the meantime I should like to remind the house that all United Nations peace keeping operations have developed largely as a result of the interpretation of a mandate to meet actual requirements. The United Nations had the same temporary difficulties that are being encountered in connection with this matter when it set up a peace force in the Suez area, and again when it set up the peace force for the Congo. Ultimately, in the case of the Congo operation-and it took longer in the Congo than I think it will take in connection with the Cyprus effort-the secretary general issued a detailed set of operational

procedures which dealt in particular with the right of self defence, and the right to shoot in self defence.
With its experience of peace keeping operations the United Nations is, I believe, well placed to judge what peace keeping methods should be applied in Cyprus, and it goes without saying that these methods will be the subject of consultation between the UN and the governments participating in the military operation. Those consultations are going on at the moment. They are going on, as far as Canada is concerned, between the secretary general and our Secretary of State for External Affairs. I understand that the secretary general will be in a position within a very few days to make a report to the security council in which some of these difficulties will be outlined and the solutions made known. We are in consultation with him at the moment with regard to this particular statement as well.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING
speechtext: I take it, then, from the Prime Minister's statement that in the event of any hostilities breaking out in Cyprus, it would probably be United Kingdom troops which would actually be engaged rather than Canadian troops at the present time.

subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING
speechtext:
Well, the Canadian contingent of the United Nations force is engaged already in the sense that it has begun patrolling activities. In the event of hostilities breaking out the function, if any, which the Canadian contingent would perform would depend entirely on the nature of the hostilities.
I am sorry I cannot go into this matter in greater detail today. I wish I could. I am not trying to hold anything back from the house in connection with this important matter. However, I shall be in a much better position to make a fuller statement when I have had another opportunity of consulting with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if indeed he is not back in the house to make a statement himself.

speechtext:

speechtext: May I direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of the declaration made by a representative of the U.S.S.R. on Saturday that the Soviet union will never pay its assessment to the United Nations for the Congo and Middle East forces, and that any challenge to its right to vote in the general assembly on that account may break up the United Nations. In view of this statement of defiance of the United Nations, and the responsibilities assumed by the U.S.S.R., and the declaration of the international court of justice that these peace keeping costs should be borne by the membership, what is the attitude of Canada in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REFUSAL TO SHARE COST OF PEACE
speechtext:
I read this report, and I share my right hon. friend's concern over it. Perhaps I could make a very short statement on the matter.
As the house is aware from previous reports that have been made to it, effective January 1, 1964, the Soviet union and a number of other member states of the United Nations became vulnerable to the application of article 19 of the charter, mainly through their failure to pay their assessed share of peace keeping costs of the United Nations. The application of this article, which provides for the loss of voting in the general assembly for members whose payments are in such arrears, will take effect when the general assembly next meets unless steps have been taken to liquidate the arrears.
The Soviet statement to which my hon. friend has referred is a further indication of the Soviet union's refusal to contribute to the financing of peace keeping operations. This manoeuvring for position, and that is what it is, in relation to a most important issue in the United Nations is being studied very closely by the government because of its implications for future effectiveness of the United Nations and the discussion of proposals for the financing of peace keeping operations, and also because of the position that will arise at the United Nations assembly when it may be necessary to apply-and it is a very serious step to take-this particular article to the Soviet union and other members of the United Nations who are in arrears.

subtopic: REFUSAL TO SHARE COST OF PEACE
speechtext:
I share with the Prime Minister his feelings in this regard. I should like to know from him what is the attitude of the Canadian government in connection with this matter. Can any member of the
Inquiries of the Ministry United Nations, by unilateral action, refuse to be bound by its pledged agreement? If so, this would place the United Nations in a position of division as between those who will assume their responsibilities and those who will not, which would result in a complete negation of the charter and the agreements that have been entered into. What representations has the government of Canada, as a middle power within the United Nations, made to the U.S.S.R. in this connection? subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 20, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the budget debate one naturally thinks of last year's budget, which the minister termed a face the facts budget. He had no name at all for this budget, and I think that was very appropriate. However, if one looked for a name one might call it a do nothing budget. Many people have hung different phrases on it, but I rather like the description put on it by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), "a thin sandwich with very little meat in it". I wonder how his party will vote when their turn comes to declare whether or not they support the budget. I suppose they will think that a thin sandwich is better than none.
When one thinks of last year's budget and this year's budget from the point of view of their effect on the economy of Canada, one finds many surprising things. I immediately think of the increase in our total debt. No one minds going in debt if they are accomplishing something by doing so. Last year's budget caused an increase in the per capita national debt of 4.2 per cent. Yet my hon. friends of the Social Credit party, who so often tell us about the dangers of going into debt, voted for it. This year's budget will bring about an increase in the total amount of Canada's debt larger than in any other year going back nearly as far as the war years. There will be an increase of over $1 billion in the total national debt in 1963-64 brought about by this budget. Yet the Social Crediters will probably vote for this highest increase in the per capita debt in Canada going back as far as 1954.
In 1954 per capita debt in Canada was something like $727. In 1955 it was cut to $717, and we reduced it to a little over $600 in 1960. In 1963 it was $736, but this coming year it will rise to $789, an increase of $50 for each Canadian. Yet my friends, the Social

Crediters from Alberta, who hate debt and talk against debt, will in all likelihood vote for this huge increase.
One can only take from this that they talk one thing and vote another. They have become so degenerate with this procedure of talking one way and voting another that they are very two-faced, to say the least. Two weeks ago in this house they voted against an amendment which we introduced during the debate on the throne speech, to provide family allowances up until the age of 18 years, but when the final vote is taken on the budget they will probably vote in favour of extending the age limit.
This perhaps points out that an erosion of democracy is setting in, particularly in that party. When people vote one way and then the opposite way, all within a two week period, one must realize there is great danger when they value their vote so lightly. This is an erosion of the very democracy in which we participate.
We on this side of the house are not afraid to borrow money and have budget deficits, so long as those deficits go to the building of the country and to improving its economy. During our term in office we built dams, vocational schools, the Pine Point railroad, power projects, helped shipbuilding and provided roads to resources in the north. We also paid more to the provinces on a very equitable basis. If anyone doubts that, let him look at the report of the recent federal-provincial conference where the tables show that between 1956 and 1963 amounts paid by the federal government to the provinces increased threefold. In 1956 the provinces received something like $600 million and in 1962-63 they received nearly $2 billion from the federal government.
Anyone can talk about deficits, but if he examines how the money was spent he would not mind borrowing money used to develop the country and to give the provinces a greater share in participating in its development. In the present budget we see an increase in taxes with another huge deficit, and we wonder what the government is doing with the money. For one thing it has been increasing salaries all around. The top echelons in the C.B.C., civil service and the armed forces have all received tremendous pay increases but the lower echelons have received very little.
One may well ask where the present buoyancy of the economy came from, but if we look at the Bank of Canada's report for 1963 we find this statement on page 7:
The over-all performance of the Canadian economy in 1963 was encouraging. Substantial increases in output and employment were achieved for a third consecutive year-

I emphasize those words "third consecutive year." It goes on to say:
Further gains were made by Canadian manufactured goods in 1963 both in export markets and in competition with imports in the Canadian market-
Why was this the third consecutive year of improvement? The report goes on to give the reason as directly because of the devaluation of the dollar.
One development that has contributed a great deal to the Canadian economy's performance in recent years has been the improvement in Canada's international competitive position. This was greatly strengthened by the decline in the foreign exchange value of the Canadian dollar in 1960-62, and as Canadian prices and costs have risen only modestly since, this advantage has been largely retained.
Certainly here is an unbiased, unpolitical, factual report on the economy of Canada which shows why our economy has remained strong for the last three years. But we must remember that all is not clear and that dangers do arise. We must maintain this position. In other words we cannot have the cost of living increasing to the point where it will eventually erode the advantages we have obtained by the devaluation of the dollar.
At page 8 the Bank of Canada report goes on to say:
At the same time the competitive position of a number of important trading countries, notably the countries of western Europe, has been weakened by the strong upward pressure on costs and prices that they have been experiencing.
In other words, we can only retain the advantages we have received from the devaluation of the dollar if we safeguard and are ever watchful of our cost of living and see to it that costs of production do not rise too far.
Further on in the report, dealing with economic developments in Canada, it says:
Average output per person employed in the non-farm sector of the economy increased by approximately 1 per cent, somewhat less than in 1962.
In other words there already is some slight eroding of the situation which followed devaluation of the dollar, and we must look to the budget for some efforts to stop this erosion. We have had a strong economy for three years because of the devaluation of the dollar, and particularly in 1963 because of the huge wheat sales. The Bank of Canada report makes reference to those wheat sales, saying they helped our foreign exchange position immensely and without them we would be in dire trouble.
As a matter of fact the Minister of Finance made some reference to this in his budget speech, but I can think back to the time when we initiated huge wheat sales to communist
The Budget-Mr. J. H. Horner China. We were condemned from various sides of the house. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), and his colleague the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson)- though I am not sure if he is still his colleague because that party has broken up so much- said we should not be selling to the communists. The present Prime Minister said it looked terrible, cash to our friends and credit to our enemies. That is what he said when we initiated the policy of selling wheat to communist countries.
He sneered at it, but he and his colleagues are not sneering now. It was their life saver in 1963, and they admit it. It was their life saver in foreign exchange. It was their life saver in trade. It was their life saver for the whole economy of the country. I looked for something in the budget which would indicate that they intended to add to the continuity of their own life saver. I looked for measures intended to help the western economy. There was nothing. While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) was reading his budget speech, I interjected: "Nothing for the farmers", and he replied, "Yes, they have children, too". No doubt the concessions with regard to education will benefit many people. But we were looking for something which would bring solid benefit to the economy as a whole.
I have here an article which appeared in the Financial Post of March 14 under the heading: "Behind the Big West Coast Grain Back-up". What is behind it? We know that because of a shortage of facilities on the west coast Canada lost the sale of 118 million bushels of wheat. I looked for something in the budget to show that the federal government was aware of this problem and that it planned to spend so many millions of dollars to improve harbour facilities out there. Again, I saw nothing to this effect. The article in the Financial Post of March 14 says the reason for the grain back-up on the west coast is the fact that facilities are inadequate and outmoded; they need improvement and extension and it is suggested that $20 million would do the job. Nevertheless, this government failed to recognize the ever increasing need for improved port facilities to handle the requirements of a trading nation such as ours. Hon. members opposite talk of foreign exchange; they talk about the need for trade. But they do very little about these things and the budget itself did absolutely nothing in this regard.
We heard the Liberals in western Canada spout off for years advocating the theory of free trade in this country. They said free trade was the answer to all our problems. When the former prime minister, my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) told Great Britain she must honour Canada's

The Budget-Mr. J. H. Horner
rights to trade with her before she entered the European common market, he was criticized and told this was not the proper attitude to take. But what about the attitude now being taken by those who sit on the treasury benches? I have here an article from the Ottawa Journal of March 17, 1964, which says:
Tariff board recommendations on oilfield equipment have been worked into the customs tariff and there is an upward trend in protection for Canadian producers of machinery and parts.
Note the words "an upward trend in protection". I am not against this, but here you have a party which for years has advocated free trade. The world has grown smaller, they said, and free trade is inevitable. It would be rough on certain industries in this country, but we had to face up to competition the world over. That was what they said for so many years. However, a different tune is being played today by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp).
The former minister of agriculture the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) was criticized with regard to the wheat sales. He was criticized for telling farmers in western Canada a year ago to grow all the wheat they could because he had found markets for that wheat. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce has yet to advise the farmers as to the size of the market he can foresee for the future. The seeding season is not far away. I am sure many farmers wonder what they should be planting. But no advice comes from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) probably because he does not know whether this matter comes within his jurisdiction; he is in a quandary and we in western Canada cannot blame him. The Minister of Trade and Commerce could at least come out and make his statement and let us judge how close he comes in his prediction.
We see very little in this budget. The minister told us, in his speech, about the importance of tourism and the beneficial effect of receipts from tourism on our balance of payments figures. Why has there been this improvement? It is the consequence of the devaluation of the dollar. This is the same dollar that was derided by hon. members opposite when it was introduced. They derided it and called it a Diefendollar, and so on. Today they are forced to recognize that it has been their life saver, along with huge sales of wheat. We looked in this budget for something for agriculture. We even looked at the last budget again to see whether there was something in it that we had

missed. In this connection let me read a paragraph from the Globe and Mail of June
15	which said, about that performance:
There are no worth-while tax cuts, no incentives
to stimulate growth and employment. The budget confesses its dismal failure in this direction by forecasting a gain of only 5 per cent in the gross national product this year, compared to the 8 per cent achieved last year by the much despised Conservatives.
We wondered what the minister would predict for this year. He said it was 5 per cent last year because of the heavy grain crops in western Canada. He said there would turn out to be an increase in the gross national product of nearly 6 per cent in 1963 because of fortunate growing conditions in western Canada. Well, in 1962 there was an increase of 8 per cent. In 1963 it was close to 6 per cent. And in 1964, the hon. gentleman says, it should be 5 per cent. Are we not moving in the wrong direction? Eight, six, five-where are we going? Is it to be four, three, two, and one by 1970? I maintain we must look forward to the future with greater optimism than this. We must bring about conditions which will create a greater growth in our gross national product than appears likely from the sliding scale which is set before us today.
We had been curious about the present budget. Well, it came, and the newspapers wrote it up. I have some comments here from one of them, the Ottawa Journal, under the headings "Little to Cheer (or Jeer) About", "Students Take the Plums", and so on. It is true there were noteworthy measures for the benefit of students and I was pleased to see them. I was glad to see that eligibility for family allowances is to be extended. But these are small matters compared with the over-all economy of the country. There was very little, if anything, in the budget for labour. There was nothing in the budget for the average businessman, nothing for the farmer. This was a dismal budget, to say the least.
We had heard a great deal about defence costs. We had heard that the minister of defence was slashing this and slashing that in an effort to pare down defence spending. Yet there turned out to be an increase in this department. Then we were told that the paring down of defence costs had yet to come. I notice, however, that it is planned to buy
16	Hercules transport planes made in the United States. We are also buying personnel carriers all of which have been manufactured in the United States. How will measures such as these strengthen our economy? We are told, of course, that defence sharing arrangements will be worked out later. But how can they be worked out when we are paring costs all round? It is the intention to build a highly mobile force, and I am in

agreement with that proposition. But I am also here to watch over the development o f our country as a whole, and the field of defence production has been one of the vital areas in which a government can act. It is true the previous government bought planes from the United States, but we had aircraft manufactured in Canada, too. Certainly this will add nothing to the economy of this country.
We looked for tax cuts in building, and we saw none. The minister said these cuts were not needed, that building had gone on anyway. Well, if we had not had the large grain sales, and if there had not been such large grain crops, our gross national product would have probably increased by less than 5 per cent.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before going any further, I should like to introduce the following amendment to the amendment:
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe):
That all the words in the amendment after "any effective action to" be deleted and replaced by: "reduce the national defence budget, so that family allowances could be adjusted to the cost of living index."
You will note that we have been insisting strongly, since the beginning of this session, on such an adjustment of family allowances
[Mr. Horner (Acadia) .1

to the cost of living index. Indeed if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is able to require of the Canadian people that they pay $1 billion 35 million interest on the national debt alone for the service of the debt, we consider that the same amount, without the creation of any more money in Canada, would enable him to raise family allowances to $22 for each Canadian child.
I have no intention of repeating the remarks made by the spokesmen of other political parties during this debate. As did the Minister of Finance, they all remained true to the most orthodox principles. No one dared to get away from the beaten track of a system poisonous to all Canadians and which deprives them of a sounder economic life.
Personally, I intend to stray off the beaten path and refrain from repeating those hollow formulas handed to us each year with the white paper on the economic health of this country and the budget set down by the government.
We, of the Ralliement Creditistes, for instance, disagree completely with the Minister of Finance. As a matter of fact, we do not accept one of the first comments he made in his budget speech when he defined what he called the first goal of the Canadian government:

Our first goal is high level employment, the highest we can expect to reach and maintain:

We, of the Ralliement Creditistes, feel that that should not be the first objective of the federal government.
We believe that the chief aim of economic activity should not be to provide jobs but to meet consumer needs.
This is what Jean Daujat, a great French sociologist wrote in his book "Reponses chre-tiennes a des problemes d'aujourd'hui":
The purpose of economic activity is not to provide jobs but to ensure the welfare of the family and of its members, that is the welfare of consumers.
After the economist manner, we would say with Rev. Father Georges-Henri Levesque, former director of the social science faculty at Laval University, in Quebec city:
Economic activities are intended for the benefit of all consumers. Consumers first and foremost. Such should be the principle of any social and truly human policy.
In 1960, the assembly of the United churches of Scotland asked a group of economists, theologians and sociologists to make a survey of the present financial structure in relation to Christian doctrine.
The committee report was made public in 1962 after being presented to the general

assembly of the United churches in Dundee, Scotland, on May 10, 1962. Later on, it was published under the title "Money, a Christian View", with a foreword by Right Rev. George F. MacLeod, former moderator of the general assembly of the Church of Scotland.
Unanimously, the authors of the report stated on page 11:

There has grown the idea that any employment is better than none and that the primary object of an economic system is to provide employment. We believe that the object of production is consumption and that while human employment is generally a necessary part of the process directed to this end it must not take precedence over it. From a Christian point of view it is wrong that a man must be employed on work that can be done by a machine-
-as we see today right across Canada.

Is the government the least concerned about the consumers' interests? Is the government taking steps to assure the distribution of goods produced to all consumers so as to give them a fair subsistence and decent living conditions? Is the government taking the means to remove financial obstacles that prevent the goods and services produced by Canadians from fully meeting the needs of Canadian consumers?
We must answer in the negative to all these questions.
But why? Why are Canadian consumers, Canadian families deprived of goods and services made available by our natural resources, our industries and workers and displayed in our stores, groceries and warehouses? Why are hundreds of industries and factories operating at reduced capacity or closed? Why are there in Canada at the present time-March 1, 1964-487,000 unemployed, 487,000 minds, 974,000 unemployed arms when thousands and thousands of families are undernourished, ill-clothed and ill-housed?
The answer is simply that the Canadian consumers do not have enough money to buy, at current prices, the goods and services which are offered them.
In a sensational book published in the middle of the depression, that is in 1934, by the Brookings Institute of the United States, Mr. Harold G. Moulton, who was one of President Roosevelt's economic advisers, wrote after an analysis of the economic situation:
-unsatisfied desires of American consumers are at the present time great enough to absorb a production higher than that of 1929. Taking into consideration the necessaries of life of the great mass of the people, innumerable needs remain unsatisfied. The problem is not one of lack of desire, but of lack of buying power.
The Budget-Mr. Caouette

The trouble is clearly not a lack of desire but a lack of purchasing power.

Moulton wrote in his book "America's Capacity to Consume" can be found in the library of parliament, for those who would like to refer to it.
A few years later, that is in 1939, an outstanding British industrialist, director of Vickers for 22 years, director of the London Insurance Company and governor of the Bank of England for nine years, wrote the following on page 50 of a book entitled "Economic Tribulation" which can also be found in the library of parliament.

If the producers are waiting to produce more, if ships are waiting to carry the goods, if there are railway and transport services wheresoever there is a demand for them, then the fault must lie with the consumer. Why does he hold back the trade and commerce and progress of the world and prevent the consummation of a lasting peace by deliberately refusing to avail himself of the good things the world can offer him?
The answer is obvious. The consumer cannot afford to buy more; he has not enough money. Let us discard all biased opinions and we shall find it possible only to arrive at one decision- that the health and welfare of the individual, the happiness of the community, the contentment of the nation and the peace of the world are mainly, if not entirely, a monetary problem.

After those findings by the group of economists of the Brookings institute, by Vincent Cartwright Vickers who was governor of the Bank of England, let us see now what the economists, theologians and sociologists of the churches of Scotland, which I quoted a moment ago, think of this situation. On page 40 of their report, they come to the same conclusions as the Social Crediters-the same conclusions as the Social Crediters, Mr. Speaker-namely, that there is a deficit in purchasing power. Here is how they say it:

The present system does not provide any mechanism by which the supply of purchasing power is automatically geared to the volume of real wealth produced. The classical theory that when goods outrun purchasing power prices will automatically fall to the proper level is bound to break down under present conditions, since the lower level of prices is determined by costs and total costs are determined by the volume of credit issued for production, which must be repaid out of prices.
The principal argument between the orthodox and the unorthodox economists appears to revolve around this point. In the view of the first, the monetary system is merely a reflection of the physical economic system, and there is no question in normal circumstances of purchasing power being in short supply. Such discrepancies as arise are the result of temporary fluctuations that are, or can be, quickly corrected. The monetary reformers for the most part maintain that there
1368	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
is a "built-in" flaw in the present system of bank credit accounting that results in a permanent shortage of purchasing power in relation to the total prices of goods offered for sale.

Not only does the report acknowledge the lack of purchasing power, it gives the reasons therefor.
I should like to quote what the authors had to say on page 29 of the same book, after the study they made of the operation of the banking system and of the creation of credit by the banks:

We cannot see any moral justification for the levying of interest on a bank loan which is, as all the experts now agree, "created out of nothing". When a bank "creates" credit in this way, neither it nor any of its customers surrenders title or claim to goods and services, nor do they abstain from "present consumption". Moreover, the addition of interest to the original bank loans, when these loans are the sole source of purchasing power, is a clear cause of purchasing power shortage. Whether or not then the function of "creating credit", that is, of issuing money, reverts in its entirety to the state, as recommended in the preceding paragraph, there cannot be any justification for the levying of a charge for this service beyond a sum sufficient to cover clerical and other costs.

Mr. Speaker, is it simply a question of theories based on Christian requirements or do these findings also take into account economic and banking data?
If you are in doubt, Mr. Speaker, may I quote the testimony of a French Canadian economist, Dr. Rosario Cousineau, director of the commerce department at the University of Sherbrooke, who stated in 1959 before the convention of the chamber of commerce of the province of Quebec, concerning the power entrusted with the chartered banks to create credit, the following, and I quote:
Without intending to take part in the controversy as to whether or not the banks create money, we can state that they create credit, that they multiply their deposits-and their equity- by 10 or 15. Provided they find creditworthy borrowers, they multiply their loans and create credit to the full extent that their loans exceed the total of their deposits and equity.
The title of this study by Dr. Cousineau was "Inflation", the very thing the monetary system itself implies, inflation, about which Grits and Tories, as well as my good friend from St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), are so much afraid when they speak of Social Credit.
Do you want other proofs of what Social Crediters have been claiming and shouting throughout Canada for a number of years?
I could give you hundreds of statements concerning the theory of the creation of credit in the banks. Let me mention, as a reminder to the hon. members of the house, just this 

book by Harold G. Moulton, economic adviser to President Roosevelt, who explains from pages 77 to 90 of his book entitled "The Formation of Capital", which is found in the library of parliament, how commercial banks make credit.
He shows, in clearly written pages I would not hesitate to claim as my own, how chartered banks, with an authorized capital of $1 million, are able to loan, even if they do not net any deposit, $100 million.
With a mere stroke of the pen, banks create the credit that they lend afterwards at interest, requiring repayment of capital which they never issue plus interest, so that there is a constant and ever increasing deficit in the purchasing power. That is the cause of our national debt of $1.37 billion, in addition to the loans that have to be made in order to hide the coming deficit.
Mr. Speaker, the consequences of such a financial system under which credit is first created by banks and then lent at interest, are obvious and have been proved. One has only to consider the gradual indebtedness of all governments, the indebtedness of corporations and of individuals, and the great number of commercial bankruptcies.
Such a system leads to the degradation of the individual, to the absolute control of the country and its economy by a small group of financiers and to personal wealth at the expense of the majority of Canadians.
It was not without reason that Pius XI stated:
Those who control the economic life blood of the country have become the masters of our lives and without their permission no one has the right to breathe.
Without the permission of those who control the economic life blood of the country, the Minister of Finance is unable to breathe and the federal government cannot breathe either because those people control the economic and political life of the country, indeed all forms of activity in Canada.
At the present time-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would, nevertheless appeal to your generosity for granting me the three minutes you just took away in order to inform me of the procedure to be followed. I shall naturally comply with the standing orders.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, 1 would, if I had the time, prove to you, on the basis of statistics, that each Canadian citizen's debt in regard to the federal debt, to the provincial debt, and to the liabilities of schools and individuals, amounts to more than $3,000, and that this debt goes on increasing from year to year because of a banking system which wants all money in circulation to represent a liability for Canadian citizens.
In table 11, which is on page 27 of the white paper tabled by the Minister of Finance, we see that, for the last four years, the service of the public debt cost Canadians $5,849 million, which is more than five times the total budget of the state of Quebec.
Under the present system, everybody gets into debt. These are among others, the headlines we read practically every day in the press, in the Toronto as well as the Montreal and Winnipeg papers:
Bankruptcy here, and another bankruptcy there .. .The schoolboards are on the verge of disaster if their finances are not put on a sounder basis...
Some municipalities are depressed, economically and financially.. .They can no longer balance their budgets.
They can no longer make both ends meet, even in Ottawa and in the provinces.
Why is there so much discontent, so much dissatisfaction? Because, due to expenses that must be incurred, the budget cannot be balanced not because physical possibilities are lacking, but because credit is totally wanting. Mr. Speaker, who profits from the present financial system? Who gets rich when governments, municipalities, school boards and individuals constantly get into debt?
Those who get rich are the bankers. The proof is to be found in the March 11, 1964 edition of the newspaper La Presse, in an article signed Laurent Lauzier, under the title:
The financiers put down their stakes.
This was written not long ago, to wit, on March 11.
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
The article closes with these words:
When the financial community thus gets into action, it is because it feels the imperative need to fashion the new frameworks which are in the offing in order to safeguard or to extend its field of action.
And yet, when those financiers want the passage of bills, we agree. Or perhaps the government will ask us to grant bank charters to new organizations, in order to allow even a greater number of financiers to exploit the Canadian people.
For instance, at present, bank charters are being asked and pressure is being exerted on parliament for the passage of legislation to allow the establishment of new chartered banks in the country.

The most significant seems to be the possibility of a revision of the Bank Act which would enhance the profitability of banking.

They do not make enough profit; they want more.

I should like to quote once again the excellent report of economist-theologians who say that without a monetary reform, it is impossible to believe in the economic, political and financial liberation of a country or a province.
That leads me to discuss what is happening nowadays in the province of Quebec. Last Friday afternoon, I heard the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) speak about separatists and insinuate that I did not speak the same language in the English speaking provinces as in the French speaking province.
For the information of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, I get more invitations from English speaking provinces that he ever received in his whole life. I meet students in English speaking universities and what I tell them, I shall repeat it here, in this parliament, this afternoon. I say the same thing in Quebec, in Ontario and in western Canada. If we are complaining in Quebec that the province is 25, 20 or 15 years behind the other provinces, as regards economic development, it is not the fault of the English speaking people in Toronto or Winnipeg.
It is because of French Canadians from the province of Quebec the Napoleonic code, while people with no guts instead of sending aggressive people to defend their interests.

Nobody will have me believe that if the province of Quebec did not develop, it is because of other Canadian people of different origins. I never asserted that.
But I know that in the province of Quebec it is possible to proceed by ourselves to our development.
At this time, we hear more and more of the reformation of the constitution, and we are asked by English Canadians from Ontario as well as from western Canada: But what do you want in the province of Quebec to leave us alone so that we will no longer hear about separatism, independence, etc.?
Mr. Speaker, in 1867, when the constitution was written, both elements in Canada were represented; for instance, education was separated, leaving to the province of Quebec its own education system, the civil code was also separated-and we will keep in the province of Quebec the Napoleonic code, while there is something else in Ontario-lines of separation were established at that time and differences were made between the two major ethnic groups in Canada.
What do we want in 1967? The assimilation of other provinces to Quebec? No, Mr. Speaker, I would be the first one to object to the assimilation of any province to the province of Quebec.
We want, when the new Canadian constitution is amended, that some other factors should be considered which will enable the province of Quebec, as well as the other provinces, to expand in a normal way. It is for that reason that we believe and urge that the new constitution should allow the provinces, and the province of Quebec as far as we are concerned:
1.	Credit control. Once we control our credit, it will not rest with the federal Minister of Finance to tax us as he is compelled to do at present to pay tribute to a financial system and to those who control the economic blood of the nation. DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SECRETARIAT
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of the immediate establishment of a secretariat for federal-provincial relations or a similar institution.

He said: Mr. Speaker, if I recommend today the immediate establishment of a secretariat or of a body of that kind, to improve federal-provincial relations, it is not to revive the classical debate on centralization as opposed, for instance, to provincial autonomy. Everyone recognizes, I think that under our constitution we must have strong governments at the federal, provincial and municipal levels, and that each of them must discharge its own responsibilities.
We recognize today that the spirit of cooperative federalism requires a high degree of consultation with the provinces. It is thus nowadays, as far as the techniques of modern governments are concerned, which imply a notion of planning. In a federal state, without close and continuous consultation, there is bound to be chaos. For the federal government to have the courtesy to resort to consultation in matters directly or indirectly affecting provincial jurisdiction does not imply any idea of retreat or abdication of responsibilities on its part.

I recognize the fact that the Prime Minister has set up some sort of mechanism within the privy council to deal with such matters and that he himself is now personally responsible to parliament for those questions.
I am absolutely convinced that the preparation of federal-provincial conferences, especially in the taxation field, is marked by a lack of co-operation and consultation.
The government should immediately study the ARDA procedure and the findings made in the field of resources. It remains to be seen whether such an organization or secretariat should be general in its nature and should include all questions directly or indirectly involving both levels of government or whether, at the outset, secretariats should be established on a departmental basis.
It is urgently necessary to emphasize consultation on a continuous and co-ordinated basis. The establishment of such an organization or secretariat will not be conducive to the breaking up of our country. But it will contribute to strengthen the ties of confederation.
Obviously, I do not want to exaggerate, it will not solve all problems in this field, but I firmly believe that it will be a practical and fruitful initiative of such a nature as to strengthen unity in diversity.

Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks this afternoon may I say I recognize it would be inappropriate at this stage to go into too much detail relating to the establishment of a secretariat or other body for federal-provincial relations, but at the same time I would like to offer a few suggestions, which I hope will be practical, relating to the establishment of such a body.
Many of us know after confederation came into being in 1867, Sir John A. Macdonald actually appointed a secretary of state for federal-provincial affairs. He, at that time, recognized the real necessity to strengthen the bonds of national unity and the bonds, so to speak, of confederation. I believe that necessity exists once more today.
Far too many people are making what I term negative declarations concerning the state of our national unity and the state of our confederation. For a number of years I have discussed, both inside and outside this house, the matter of the establishment of this secretariat or a similar body. I know there is a need today for this approach, and I hope it will constitute a practical step forward in unifying our country. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I hope my resolution and the subject matter contained therein will meet with the general approval of all members of the house.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
I note with a great deal of pleasure that when meeting in Ottawa with the premiers of the provinces a few weeks ago, the Prime Minister expressed general agreement on the subject matter of the resolution I have introduced. I note too with equal pleasure that many of the provincial premiers also expressed general agreement with the terms of this resolution.
As I have already stated, we have had great and useful experience in the secretariat having to do with federal-provincial relations in the resources field. Most members of the house and most of the people of Canada were very interested recently when the Prime Minister established a body of personnel in the privy council offices for federal-provincial affairs. The Prime Minister recognizes the basic, great importance of this subject in that he answers to this house on questions put to him regarding problems existing between Ottawa and the provinces.
Even though I shall now be going into a certain amount of detail, I should like to mention that there was general agreement at the last federal-provincial conference, between the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers, that the time has come to establish a secretariat on the prime minister and premiers level. The Prime Minister and the provincial premiers could form a prime minister and premiers council for federal-provincial relations, and a secretariat could then be formed, similar to the one in the resources field, which would report its findings to the council composed of the Prime Minister and premiers.
The council and secretariat would, of course, be keynoted by a high degree of co-operation and continuous consultation. At the same time, even if such a secretariat were established, we would still have to encourage an increased degree of continuous consultation on a departmental or, if you will, ministerial level. The council of the Prime Minister and premiers, and the secretariat, would cover the general field of federal-provincial relations, and they would have an important co-ordinating function based on continuous consultation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) with his experience in international affairs recognizes that if one enters upon international conferences without adequate preparation, the results are often likely to be disappointing. We have seen this happen often when disarmament has been the subject of such conferences. If such discussions are to have the best chance of success, a great deal of work must be done beforehand in connection with the details of the subject matter; there must be consultation beforehand with those concerned. In other words,

Dominion-Provincial Relations there is a good deal oi homework to be done. The same notion should be the keynote of federal-provincial relations-this idea of continuous and co-ordinated consultation.
In carrying out the recommendations and suggestions that I have put before the house today, a minimum of personnel would be desirable and a minimum of personnel would be required. No empire building is contemplated. No superbody would be established which might possibly lead to an invasion of federal or provincial authority either at the legislative or at the administrative level.
I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that these suggestions will commend themselves to all hon. members and that they will prove useful. Alluding to what I have already said, may I express the hope that they will have a practical and positive unifying effect in our country today, at a time when too many people are making what I consider to be negative, destructive declarations. For this reason I hope that the resolution and the subject matter contained therein will meet with the approval of all hon. members in each and every party, and that the motion will be adopted this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the topic of this motion is one that has been of much interest and concern to those in this party and to me personally. On two occasions in previous sessions I have introduced a motion to set up a permanent, full scale ministerial department of government to deal with the matter of federal-provincial affairs. I appreciate the resolution that is now before us, introduced by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). I appreciate, also, the non-partisan way in which the hon. member spoke. It is with a good deal of pleasure that we give our support to this motion. I do believe it would be more constructive if members of the government would be just a little more positive in their remarks regarding the motion and would say whether they are for or against it.
I have just been checking over some of the remarks made last year with regard to this subject, and I think it might be well if we were to refresh our memories on certain aspects of it which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi did not really bring out in his remarks. Confederation was a coming together of the provinces. We have heard a great deal about co-operative federalism. I think one of the reasons we have as many problems as we do today in Canada is simply that we have not lived up to the spirit of the original confederation. What is needed today -while we do give credit for as much cooperative federalism as has been indicated by the government-is a greater degree of cooperative federalism based upon the concept of confederation of 100 years ago. Basically this original concept of confederation was an agreement among the provinces to form a nation, Canada. There was to be a federal form of government. Canada was to be a nation that not only maintained its independence as far as its relationships with the United States were concerned, but also with the mother country, and other colonial countries across the sea. I think that if our federal administration could establish a greater degree
1374	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations of co-operation in those various fields which overlap between provincial and federal responsibility, and if there could be a greater amount of co-ordination, we would really have a greater sense of unity and national spirit in Canada.
It is true that provincial governments lead the way in this particular field. A number of provincial governments have actually set up departments to deal with federal-provincial affairs. I believe, as the record will show, they have found these departments to be very useful. This does not only apply in the field of resources but it applies in regard to one of the most critical problems that we face today as far as federal-provincial relations are concerned. I refer to the field of taxation. Certainly many of the fiscal problems that we have today would not be there if we had a greater degree of understanding relating to the shared cost programs which have developed in recent years.
Another aspect of our national development that is very important at the present time is a national highways program. We will never have the national highways program that this country needs unless it is done on the basis of co-ordinated understanding and co-operation with the provinces. The same problem exists with regard to education and health. We maintain that education and health are basic responsibilities of the provinces; yet there are fields within education and health which just cannot be divided into as many compartments as we have provinces. The basic problem which faces all educational departments in the different provinces relates to the question of money and the co-ordination of programs which affect the entire nation. Therefore it is my opinion, as I have thought over the establishment of such an organization on the federal scene, that probably the first step toward a full scale ministerial department of government would be the setting up of a secretariat such as is now being suggested.
It is on this basis that we give our full support to the motion before us. We trust that the government members who are yet to speak will consider this matter in the light of the tremendous importance of the topic with which we are now dealing. It seems to me that such a secretariat would not only eliminate many of the problems which face the government at this time, but it would also prepare and pave the way for a better understanding with regard to some of the problems which are not yet at the critical stage. Still other problems can be anticipated, and certainly there would be a greater sense of national spirit and unity than we have at the present time if the subject matter of this motion were put into effect.


I do not wish to deal with this subject at any great length, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that we as members of this house, being representative of all the provinces and a cross section of political thought in this country, have as one of our most urgent responsibilities to think of and be concerned with the problem of national unity. I do not think there is any other single way through which we can develop the national unity which I believe all of us would like to see in our country, as far as government is concerned, than by the setting up of such a secretariat as is proposed. Therefore we give our support to this measure. I would urge that all hon. members take a positive attitude, not just to the motion before the house but to the whole related question of national unity in our country, thus facilitating in a tremendous way the growth of our country by working together in a more efficient and effective manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to put on record the support of our party for the intent of this motion, and we would be glad to have the opportunity of voting for it if a vote were called. The subject opens up a great many areas into which one can go. It has always been my observation that as a preliminary to a secretariat we require a much stronger prime minister's office than we have at the present time. I am not talking about the incumbent but about the office as such, although one could make some comments about the incumbent too. But as I see it, the previous prime minister had, and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has, an inadequate staff to deal with many of its relationships. It also seems to me that the prime minister's office is not only the power centre of our form of government at the present time, but it is particularly so where provincial relationships are concerned.
I do not think one could really consider a secretariat in detail without considering how it would be centred in the prime minister's office. I am also of the opinion that the privy council and its present staff should fight for its tie-in with the cabinet in ministerial meetings; but again the staff is inadequate to support the office of the prime minister. On this point, I think that anyone who wanted to find someone who could speak in French on policy in the prime minister's office at the present time would go very short. That is just one indication of how stripped is the office of the prime minister, or how barren it is at the present time; there is not one press officer who can speak in the French language and would be the opposite number of Mr. O'Hagan. I mention that as an example of the fact that

the staff of the main power centre of the administration at the present time, certainly as regards relationships with the provinces, is hopelessly inadequate; and it seems to me that any development of a secretariat at the federal level to deal with federal-provincial relations should be centred around and in the prime minister's office.
Another factor here, one which we would welcome, is that it would enable us to come much more to grips with the way that a prime minister is able to handle his responsibility to the House of Commons in respect of relationships with the provinces, where his authority at the present time seems to me to be blurred by the role of cabinet ministers and the fact that we have cabinet solidarity and secrecy. I think the reality of power at the present time is that we should see it focused more strongly in the prime minister's office and should have an opportunity to see it displayed in front of us so that we could analyse it, comment upon it and make demands upon it. I do not think we have that at the present time, and this proposal of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) would go some way toward opening up this kind of development.
Therefore we should like to go on record as approving the motion, and we should like to see whether the government could follow up in working out, in concert with other parties in the house through some kind of committee, the kind of secretariat which would be useful so as to fulfil the general intention of the hon. member's proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on that motion. First of all, I want to congratulate the sponsor, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) for introducing it.
In my opinion, if we were to achieve the object of that motion I am sure that it would help improve the situation which exists between the provinces and the federal government with regard to certain bills. At the present time, relations with the provinces are strained, more especially between the province of Quebec and the federal government, because, instead of co-operative federalism we have rather centralizing federalism. I believe that such a permanent secretariat for federal-provincial relations would tend to prevent the federal government from interfering in all sorts of fields which are none of its concern. Besides, the federal government would certainly have to consult with the provinces before introducing its budget.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
In the past, we had several examples of tensions between the provinces and the federal government. For instance, when the federal government passed municipal loans legislation, some provinces criticized that action, and rightly so.
At this time we have before us-and it was mentioned in the speech from the throne debate-a bill concerning loans to students. We all know that the province of Quebec and various organizations, even at the national level, protested against that intrusion of the central government in the field of education which belongs to the provinces.
Furthermore, with that permanent secretariat sitting all year round, some problems of joint federal and provincial responsibility could be referred to it, as, for instance, the matter of lotteries, or water pollution control which is a problem concerning the federal as well as the provincial governments.
For this reason, I think that the suggestion made in this motion is constructive. Its implementation would provide a greater respect for the provinces and assist substantially in reaching a better understanding, which in the end would promote the cause of national unity.
Those are all the remarks I had to make. I take this opportunity to add that I think the government should accept this motion and introduce a measure to set up that secretariat which would be very useful for all the provinces and for the federal government.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SECRETARIAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) I suppose hon. members expect me to speak about the national gallery. I might even venture to speak about the C.B.C., but I would imagine that some hon. member would rise and under rule 26 move the adjournment of the house. We have had the suggestion here that consultation has moved in the direction of centralizing power in this country, and that somehow or other this government has shared in that. I should like to point out with regard to the shared cost programs that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) has indicated that the federal government would co-operate in transferring some of these programs to the provincial governments. In the last few days we have witnessed a bill being introduced in the legislature of the province of Ontario in a matter relating to the Criminal Code which is a scandal and a disgrace, and if there had been consultation with the federal

Dominion-Provincial Relations government by the province in that case, Mr. Speaker, the humiliation which most Canadians feel might have been avoided.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question of consultation was well set out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on the occasion of the dominion-provincial conference last November. The chief area of consultation is that of joint responsibility. There is a fruitful field which might well be explored and developed. A very important factor is not the setting up of machinery which would be approved; the most important factor is that there be regularity of consultation. If there is regularity of consultation, it can be planned and anticipated, and there could be a meeting together and a sharing of minds. I believe one of the important things which we must develop in our provincial-federal relationship is this regularity of consultation.
A number of members have spoken about having a minister in the federal government responsible for federal-provincial matters. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) pointed out that this should be the special domain of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and thus an advantage might be gained by extending his staff so that they would be trained to deal with this problem. The Prime Minister could answer questions concerning federal-provincial problems. If we were to set up a special minister we might, in fact, encumber consultations; we might not facilitate them. We know, for instance in the international sphere there are consultations between various branches of this government and branches of government in other countries. These consultations are quite often so intimate that the normal channels of diplomacy are not the prime avenue for them. I think it is very important that we should develop easy, quick and efficient means of consultation. If this were to be accomplished through the establishment of a special minister, it might well be that this would encumber the consultations.
Each authority must set up its own machinery. It is not for us, in this house, to say what the province of Ontario, the province of Quebec or the province of Prince Edward Island should do. We must think of our own facilities. The area of consultation does not necessarily apply to the same ministry in each province. We know that the federal Department of Labour has responsibility for co-ordinating the vocational training programs and the apprenticeship programs. In point of fact, different ministries in different provinces have responsibility for both of these programs, and in some provinces responsibility is split between two ministries. You cannot always consult with one ministry


in a province in dealing with any one of these particular areas of responsibility.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) upon his presentation and to commend the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) concerning national unity in this country. We have to free ourselves from the easy going attitude we have had towards our problems, towards our responsibilities. We must respond to meet the economic challenges and to meet the other challenges which confront us as a people at all levels. The resolution of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi draws attention to the important problem of federal-provincial relations and, in my opinion, focuses attention on this important area of Canadian life which requires examination, which requires planning and which requires consultation.
We have set up an economic council which has taken over responsibility in terms of planning, and which will consult with the provinces on various areas of life in this country. This council will have channels of consultation and channels for planning. I do not believe we can crystallize all these problems in terms of one suggestion, in terms of one idea. I believe we are going to develop channels of consultation. We are going to delineate areas in which consultation can be more effectively conducted. I believe that in this manner, in a pragmatic way, by developing areas of consultation, by recognizing areas of joint responsibility, by ensuring regularity of consultation, we can facilitate the solution of problems in these important areas of our national life.
I think the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi is to be complimented for his statement, for his resolution, and I am certain that in every way we must keep continually before us the important problem of dominion-provincial relations which cuts across many areas of our national life.
