Mr. Speaker, we, in this corner of the house, would also like to give our opinion on the motion submitted by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey).
I feel that the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi deserves to be congratulated for suggesting that a secretariat for federal-provincial relations be set up.
In the past, the setting up of such an organization would have had an impact, for instance with regard to municipal loans, because without it, at one time, the federal government had to back down in order to

study the circumstances surrounding the loans to the municipalities and to give at least some measure of satisfaction to all interested parties.
In the case of the national pension scheme, for instance, the federal members were asked to consider such a plan when Quebeckers knew all the time that the Quebec government intended to introduce its own plan without the federal members for Quebec knowing anything about it. If there had been a secretariat for federal-provincial relations, then we would have known what was going to take place in Quebec, and this secretariat would have been able to co-ordinate the views of all concerned. In this way we would have been able to choose between the provincial and the federal pension plans.
The same thing goes for student loans. At present the authorities and those who are most directly concerned, the students of the province of Quebec, are against the proposed federal legislation because education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
If there had been a secretariat for federal-provincial relations, perhaps the central government would have been more cautious and would have given serious consideration to the representations made and the arguments invoked by the provinces before taking the kind of action which the present government has been initiating during the past year especially.
There is one point on which I should like to insist.
Minor details as a whole do not reveal the federal government's present policies, which are far from being consistent with understanding and agreement between the federal and the provincial governments, but there is still something more important, I think, and it is that we have been witnessing for some time federal-provincial conferences, where the federal government is endeavouring to solve the problems facing the ten provinces and we believe that on such occasions, the things at stake in the discussions are not seen in their true perspective.
Each province has problems to discuss, each province has rights to defend, especially the province of Quebec.
I believe that the discussions should no longer take place between the federal government and the ten provinces; if we mean to reach an agreement the discussions should be conducted between the federal government and the province of Quebec alone, one facing the other, as equal partners. There should not be on one side, the federal government, and on the other, the province of Quebec with the other nine provinces, because, in this case, the discussion is distorted, each province
Dominion-Provincial Relations brings in her arguments and leads the discussion according to her own wishes, and nothing is solved.
Such a secretariat for federal-provincial relations might promote discussion, not only between the ten provinces and the federal government on the one hand, but also between the federal government and the government of one province particularly concerned. If a province was faced with some problem, or wished to suggest some solutions or present some arguments, it might deal directly with the federal government and would not have to sit around a table with ten other governments, when the object of those conversations would quite often concern only that particular province and the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, this would be the only way of settling the disputes between the provinces and the federal government.
During the last federal-provincial conference, in November 1963-and the same thing will happen again at the beginning of April- we saw that when ten provinces, all with different interests, were each discussing some point of particular interest, the government was unable to settle any problem and to find any solution.
When discussions take place between the federal government and the government of each individual province, some issues will probably be settled.
I think that this federal-provincial secretariat might be charged with looking after the problems of each province. Everyone knows that the province of Quebec-and I am speaking of that province because it is my own, just as other hon. members for Saskatchewan or Manitoba will speak about wheat, because they come from the wheat growing provinces-has some particular problems to settle. If they cannot be settled at this time, it is due to the lack of a body to promote frank and sincere discussions between the Ottawa and the Quebec governments.
Mr. Speaker, I say this because I do not see how Quebec can be interested in the problems of Newfoundland, British Columbia or Manitoba. I do not see how the representatives of these various provinces, by meeting with the federal government, can discuss advisedly a given problem.
It is why I contend that such a secretariat should have as its aim to analyse the problems according to circumstances in regard to situation or location. Then, valid solutions could be arrived at which would satisfy everybody, since everyone would have the opportunity of outlining his problems and discussing them as he wished.

The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) indicated that he personally is in favour of the motion. I suspect that the reasons are diametrically opposed. I am rather surprised, I must say, that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm should take the stand that he did because as the veritable leader of his party in the province of Quebec one would have thought that as a member of this house he would have been more concerned about the jurisdiction of the federal government.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that integration of our economy and society grows apace and that co-operation of a kind never dreamed of a hundred years ago between the several branches of our governments is now necessary. This is especially true in the area of economic development. I am sure that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) wishes to propose programs for the development of Atlantic Canada he feels embarrassed by the fact that the federal government can do only certain things and must rely on the provinces to complement what he proposes in this house by their own provincial programs.
My hope would be that a federal-provincial secretariat of the kind proposed by the hon. member would strengthen the bonds of our national unity. I hope that in such a secretariat we would have the opportunity to exchange information, to become aware of the problems of the various parts of the country, and to co-ordinate our diverse plans. It seems to me that there is an error abroad in the land, and I thought I could detect it rather clearly in the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). The implication there was that Canada is a country produced by two founding races. I think this label is a useful one when we are talking about one of the problems confronting our parliament and our people at this time. But this label conceals much of the reality. Let us remember that Canada is a confederation of provinces, originally three or four with others added later. I would hope that a secretariat of this kind,

being a meeting place for the federal government and representatives of the several provinces, would emphasize the fact that this country is a federation of provinces, and that any problems of other kinds there are will be dealt with as superimposed upon this fact.
A good deal of preliminary co-operation would be necessary if such a secretariat is to be established. I do not think we in this house can presume to advise the provinces that they should set up a sector representing them in a federal-provincial secretariat. It seems to me that the hon. member for Port Arthur made a very shrewd observation concerning the Prime Minister's office. Perhaps it was only speculation, but if so it would probably be borne out by an examination of the real facts.
There will have to be a good deal of exploration with regard to what such a secretariat will accomplish before we can push ahead to devise the precise machinery of the secretariat. I think this is important to remember because such a secretariat is not without its dangers. The people of Canada are represented here now by a parliament. It would be hazardous to create another entity of government, a kind of national congress, a kind of congress of ambassadors supplanting this parliament and thereby supplanting the direct, democratic procedures on which this House of Commons is based. Nevertheless, despite these dangers I think we should explore this idea, not so that the secretariat would become a congress in effect making the law for the land, but so that it might become a place for the exchange of information and for consultation among and between the several governments in this country. speechtext:
I was going to open my remarks tonight with a few kind comments to some of my colleagues on the other side, but the particular colleagues I wish to address myself to are not here, so I shall stop the pleasantries and move on to the main purpose of my speech dealing with the budget.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) indicated that a budget should and must be more than just a government housekeeping list. He indicated that it must primarily be a document that indicates the social purpose of the government. To me this is very, very true. A budget is a document through which a political party expresses its social purpose in practical terms. It is the instrument through which the theory of its social ideals is translated into practice, and it is with this aspect of the budget I should like to deal tonight.
I realize that a budget is also so many other things, and deals with problems of trade, investment and so on. However these are things that were covered in the budget speech, and undoubtedly will be covered by other hon. members on both sides of the house, so I shall not deal with them. A budget does many things, and in the social field it has a distinct purpose. I think you can see what purpose a budget has, you can recognize the social policy when you look at a budget's approach to the way in which revenue is raised and, obviously on the other side of the coin, to the way in which moneys are spent, the level of the expenditures and the direction in which they go.
I should like to look at these particular factors in the present budget. First of all, let us look at how we raise the revenue we need. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands criticized the budget, and criticized quite severely the fact that there was no tax on capital gains. He suggested large sums were being made, large profits were being earned, and that not one nickel of this was finding its way into the public treasury. He would tax these profits thereby, in his own words, "preventing a grossly inequitable distribution of that income."
The effect of this would be to put a ceiling on the business opportunities that are available in this country. He would seek to redistribute the income in the country through taxes, in such a way that you would lift the bottom up, helping those people who need help but at the same time putting the lid on the top, or limiting the opportunities available. He would seek then to add to 20220-88
The Budget-Mr. Hahn the maxim, that all men are born equal, the words, and shall so remain.
I reject this; I think it is wrong.
It seems to me that over the years the structure of our taxation, the means we use to reap our revenue, have grown a bit lopsided. The original purposes are probably becoming a bit obscure as more needs are added year by year and more funds are needed to meet them, but we still do have an underlying philosophy within our taxation system of redistribution by progressive income and other taxes. We have remaining some incentive for private investment for capital gains, for the entrepreneur to invest money in the country, because these capital gains are not yet taxed; but the system has become blurred and confused over the years.
This year, for reasons outlined by the Minister of Finance, we are not making a change in the fundamental basis of collecting our revenue, but by the end of this year the report of the royal commission on taxation should be presented and in our next budget we should see the start of changes in our method of collecting revenue which should reflect the social purpose of the government. When we do I hope that in making these changes we recognize what we ought to do to meet our basic needs.
First of all, I think it is imperative that we always recognize the needs of those people who are not able by themselves to maintain a minimal, reasonably decent standard of living. I hope that we always continue to distribute from those that have to those that have not. We must provide means to alleviate the hard core of suffering that still exists in our country. As a Liberal these things are inherent in my philosophy. In doing this we must be very careful that we do not remove strong incentives for those who would like to invest, strong incentives for advancement and opportunity within our country.
I do not think we can attempt to follow a social pattern of trying to produce an artificial equality. We must allow room for free competitive opportunities in a free society so that people can find their own levels. I expect taxation to effect a redistribution of income, to put a floor under hardship and misery within the country. I am sure Conservative members of the Conservative party would want the same thing, although I am sure we could not agree on the level at which this floor should be. The important thing is that we must try and put this floor under misery without at the same time putting a ceiling on top of opportunity.
All men may be born equal, but I think it is folly to say they are going to die that way. So, when we revise out taxes I hope we allow, maintain, continue and probably

Now let us turn to the other side of the coin. Let us look at the spending. The Conservative amendment suggests in true Conservative fashion that we are spending too much and that our deficits are too high.

speechtext: You said we were spending too much.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hearing these Conservative
views expressed, I think there is something about the acoustics of this hall which makes those views much more palatable when they come from Mr. Speaker's left. I hope it remains that way.
What should we be trying to achieve in our levels of spending? Is it realistic to expect the absolute levels of expenditure in this country to decline? Can we really chop great chunks out of our spending? I, for one, would like to see reduced levels of expenditure, as I am sure most people would, because if we spent less it might be possible to cut taxes. But is it realistic to expect such cuts? There are only two ways, as far as I am aware, in which to cut spending. The first is by increasing the efficiency with which money is spent so as to make maximum use of every dollar. The other way in which to save money is to cut out items which are not needed.
It is unfortunate but true, I think, that governments are inherently inefficient in their spending operations. It seems to me that waste goes hand in hand with the size of the operation, which is an inescapable part of all government operations. The Glassco commission pointed this out in most definite terms. The present government is now implementing the recommendations of that royal commission and its action in so doing will increase the efficiency with which the government spends its money. We are likely to realize some attractive savings in consequence, but I do not believe that the total savings to be realized in this way will be significant or substantial enough to lead to a significant fall in government expenditure.
I think steps taken toward making the machinery of government more efficient will be both beneficial and productive but I do


not think they can be maintained to the extent of producing fundamental changes. It seems to me we must also be realistic enough to realize that, no matter which party is in power over the years, new examples of inefficiency will creep into the administration while some of the old ones we thought had been got rid of will return, despite all the efforts which were made to get rid of them. So it seems that at some stage in the future we shall be obliged to go through the whole procedure again and review once more the efficiency of our spending. It is unfortunate, but I think these problems are inherent in any government operation and I do not believe any government could count on long term substantial reductions in expenditure as a result of increasing its efficiency.
This means that the only way in which we could successfully cut expenditure, should we decide to do so, would be by reducing the number of items on which we are spending money or by reducing the amount spent on each. Last session, as a new member, I sat in this chamber during the presentation of the estimates. In my naive ignorance I thought I was witnessing the process by which parliament exercised control over the public purse strings. I expected to hear members querying various items of expenditure to find out whether they were really necessary, whether the amount spent could be reduced, and so on. As we all know, that is not what happens. There are, obviously, exceptions. But the impression I received was of a number of speeches aimed at urging the government to spend money on things which might be popular with constituents back home.
Members' sitting opposite who, in their criticism, complained by and large that we were spending too much money, failed to produce many concrete or constructive ideas as to where our spending might be cut. There were notably few suggestions from the other side of the house in this regard. Parliamentary perusal of expenditure seemed to resolve itself into general requests for more spending. The idea that parliament controls the purse strings during the examination of the estimates is not a realistic one, in my opinion, and I hope that the committee which is now studying procedures of the house will consider this particular matter and, possibly, recommend that the estimates be studied in some other way, for instance in a committee where some effective work could be carried out. If this were done we might be able to bring about some savings, though I do not think that any major savings could be effected. Thus, neither by increasing our efficiency nor by improved methods of parliamentary scrutiny are we likely to achieve substantial cuts in our spending levels.

I know that Conservatives are opposed to increases in government spending. It is a natural conservative tendency-I mean to begin that word with a small "c"-to resist such increases. However, there are still a number of fields in which there is a need for continued and even increased public expenditure. For example, I do not believe that we have by any means done all we ought to do in the field of welfare in this country. There are still far too many Canadians who are existing in living conditions which most of us would consider deplorable. There are some who say we ought drastically to slash our expenditures in this area. I should like to take them to certain parts of my own riding where they would see people living in substandard housing, ill clothed, ill fed and worried about medical bills. I am sure they would then feel, as I do, that this is not worthy of Canada in 1964. In the field of welfare therefore, if we are to satisfy my conscience at least we should be spending more, not less.
There are, in fact, a number of directions in which there is still a continuing need for public expenditures. For example, we need to direct more funds to investment in this country. We need to spend more money training people in the new technology so that they can obtain and retain employment in a technological society. We need to develop those areas of our country where unemployment remains high; we need to establish and develop industries which are capable of competing in a world where tariff changes are likely to take place. We must continue the process of investing in the human and material resources of our country-any program of this kind will mean continuing certain expenditures in the future. If we do not make these expenditures we shall, in the long term, be confronted with the need to make welfare payments on an ever increasing scale, the consequence of not having prepared ourselves for the changes which lay ahead.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) criticized the increases in expenditure associated with the new Department of Industry. This department has two main functions. One of them is area development, aimed substantially at fulfilling a definite need in this country by concentrating on those regions where unemployment is higher than it should be. These are the problem areas about which we must do something if we are to achieve a reasonable balance across the country. The department has another purpose, namely, to work with industry and assist it in reaching a position where it is competitive in the export markets which we must seek. Surely these aims are worthwhile aims and if we do not achieve them 20220-88i
The Budget-Mr. Hahn we shall suffer for it later on, since the consequence will undoubtedly be increased unemployment. It does not seem valid to me therefore, to criticize the expenditure of money for these purposes. The Atlantic development board has a somewhat similar function but I notice the hon. member was. not too critical of expenditures made in this particular area.
I think it is perfectly valid to criticize the way in which the department is carrying out its responsibilities. It is obviously too early yet to say whether it has done a good or a poor job. The basis on which it started indicates that it is doing a good job, but a few years from now there may be a very valid criticism that the department is not doing the job it should be doing. However, this is no reason to criticize the basic need of establishing a department to carry out these functions that I think had to be carried out. So that this, again, is an area where I say that spending must continue, must expand; we must continue to make expenditures in areas that are going to help the economy of the country develop for the future.
On the basis of this, then, there are many, many areas where we are not now doing the job we should be doing. There are many areas where we could be and perhaps should be, spending more, not less, than we are. So that to me the balance, the distinguishing factor, the thing that is important is that we have all these needs that we are not now meeting because we only have certain resources with which to meet them. On the basis of this I cannot see expenditure going down, in absolute terms. It is a question of at what rate will our expenditures rise.
It seems to me we have to concern ourselves with the rate of rise of our expenditures and not think in terms of absolute cuts. We have to concern ourselves with what is the right rate of rise of expenditure, in what priority, and to what things do we put the increased money which we are spending. I think in this budget we see a good example of what, to my mind, is a proper balance of these factors.
We are increasing our spending by some per cent or so; the gross national product is forecast to rise to about 5 per cent, so we are not plowing all our gains into increased expenditures. We are doing what I also feel we must do; we are using some of our gains in order to reduce the deficit. We are reducing the deficit by one third this year; we are starting to get that under control. I hope that in the future we will get the deficit wiped out. I would like to see surpluses so that we can reduce our debt load, because this is one place where we can save money in absolute terms.

The Budget-Mr. Slogan
Also, I should like to see tax cuts so there is greater incentive to Canadians. But as of now, I think the amount of spending increase that is forecast for this year relates to two things; the fact that there is always a need, and a legitimate need, for greater expenditures and the size of our deficit. In view of the gross national product increase, I think the increased expenditures forecast for this year are reasonable. Look at what we are expending these funds on. It seems to me that the type of expenditures we are making balance against the social factors that I think have to be balanced. One is providing opportunities for Canadians in terms of job retraining and educational grants in terms of employment opportunities, and through such things as the bonus on housing, the municipal loan and development fund, and all these other projects. It seems to me that by spending money in this area we are meeting the economic needs of the country.
Also, through our educational grants, through the relief of taxes to students, we are trying to provide, as I think we must, the equality of opportunity for Canadians that I think is so important and desirable. What we are not doing to the full extent that we must- and we will be doing this over the years and will always have to continue it as we get in better financial shape-is this; we must still go after the problem of substandard living conditions. But I think for this year we are moving in the right direction; we are putting our increased expenditures into those things that are needed to build up the country in the future.
So I think this budget is sound. I do not believe we should be criticized for an absolute increase in our expenditure, bearing in mind the rate of growth of the economy in relative terms and the increased percentage of gross national product. Our total expenditures are moving down and our budget deficit is coming into balance. I think the area in which we are spending is also in line with the sort of things to which I like to see increased expenditures go. So if I may quote from the well known commercial, to me the spending side of this budget is right for our times.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Monday evening, like other members of parliament and like people all across the country, I listened very attentively to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) as he brought down the budget. To say the least, it was a disappointment. Last year the minister could be called the great surgeon. He came into this great operating room of parliament and brought forth his patient, the ailing economy, and began to operate to remove the ulcers. Before he had finished, he had amputated all the patient's limbs.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And left the clamps inside.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The pundits of the Liberal party are certainly not following that course this year. The great surgeon is treating the ills of the economy with aspirins and with the occasional sugar-coated pill. Surely this is not that bold, aggressive approach that was promised to the people of Canada in the last election campaign. In fact, it seems that the front bench of this government, although so young in power, is peopled by old and tired men who lack initiative, imagination and the aggressiveness that is needed to set this economy on the right road again. Again, I must say that in listening to some of the backbenchers I thought they exhibited better insight and more common sense than the men on the front bench.
How are we supposed to judge this budget? The only criteria we can use in judging the budget are the criteria which the Liberal party themselves set in the election promises of the last campaign, and also in the criticisms of the economy as it existed under the former government. So let us look at the economy in the last year of the Conservative government. Our gross national product showed an increase of 8 per cent; one third more than in this fiscal year. Certainly, if they said that 8 per cent was not enough to get the economy moving, they should be doing something to surpass 8 per cent.
Another yardstick, of course, is the cost of living index. In 1962 the late President Kennedy said that Canada had attained the greatest price stability among all the nations of the free world. In fact, in the last three years of the Conservative administration the cost of living index was kept well below what it is this year. Therefore we not only had greater stability of price and a higher gross national product, but we had greater national production. It is the true index of growth in the economy. National production in the last year of the Conservative government was 6.4 per cent, as against 4.3 per cent last year. That, again, was almost one third higher. In the last election campaign the Liberal party said the country was standing still; they said the economy had to be put on the tracks again, it had to be set in motion. By their own standards, by their own criteria, they have failed. They have failed most miserably the people of Canada and their own party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hypocrites.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to come back to this topic a little later, Mr. Speaker. I would now like to look at some of the sugar-coated pills. One is the extension in family

allowances to children of 16 and 17 years of age who remain in school. This, of course, was part of the Conservative platform in the last election campaign. We in this party brought forth a resolution a few weeks ago, and the people on the other side of the chamber decided to vote against it. Now they bring it in. It is welcomed; it is good; we support it. Then there is the loan provision to students, which is also very much welcomed and which we support.
But we wonder what has happened to all those scholarships which the Liberal party promised the young people of Canada. There has been the exemption of tuition fees of part-time students, and I understand that this is being extended to graduates in the technical and professional fields who undertake postgraduate and refresher courses. I welcome this. I was one who over the years tried to achieve this. I also think that as well as tuition fees the cost of instruments, books, and travelling and living expenses should be included. After all, the professional man contributes a large portion of the income in the coffers of the federal treasury, and he is being penalized twice. He has not been encouraged to take refresher courses and keep abreast of advances in technology, which are in essence a capital investment for him because through his added knowledge he earns more money, which means added income to the federal treasury.
I hope the Minister of Finance will give consideration to greater exemption for postgraduate courses. It is anomalous that at the present time the professional man can go to an international or domestic convention once a year and write off all his expenses, whereas if he undertakes a refresher course, that is not possible. Inasmuch as most of these courses are undertaken in different countries or different parts of Canada, this is a real necessity.
I should now like to make a few remarks on the current account deficit in our international balance of payments. As the report of the Bank of Canada shows, in the last few years there has been a substantial decline in this deficit and there has been a welcome decline this year. As the Bank of Canada report shows, if it had not been for two factors, the devaluation of the dollar and large sales of grain to communist countries, that deficit would have been larger this year than last. Certainly here are two stories which deserve retelling. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) mentioned these factors this afternoon, and I should also like to say a little on the story of wheat.
It can truly be said that this year the farmers of the country did a great deal to attain what growth there has been in the
The Budget-Mr. Slogan economy and contributed to the improvement in our international balance of payments. When the Conservative party came to power in 1957 we inherited large surpluses of wheat, owing to the fact that the policy of the Liberal party was this: If people want our wheat, let them come and get it, because we grow the best wheat in the world. Part of the national agricultural policy of the former Conservative government was that of accelerated sales. We went out and sold wheat. Then came the Chinese wheat deal. Mr. Hazen Argue, who was the leader of the C.C.F. party and then latterly the agriculture spokesman of the Liberal party, stated that this was not a wheat deal at all because there was no fixed price, and therefore it was bad for Canada.
But was it bad for Canada? How short can memories be? We in western Canada remember how the Liberal party sold the western farmers down the river in the British wheat deal when, because of a fixed price, hundreds of millions of dollars were lost to the farmers in the west when the world market price of wheat soared. Then after that, feeling sorry for the farmers, the Liberal government of that day took $60 million from the taxpayers' pockets and distributed it amongst the western farmers, giving them a return of 10 cents on the dollar as compared with the money which could have been earned when world prices increased. When the Chinese wheat deal was negotiated the price was $1.67 a bushel. Then the price went up to over $2. You remember, Mr. Speaker, the great march on Ottawa by the western farmers who were asking for deficiency payments on grain of 30 cents a bushel. They got their deficiency payments through the increase in world prices and it did not cost the taxpayers a cent. This has been the policy of the Conservative party, and it is little wonder that the agricultural people of Canada support us.
I have been talking about agriculture and I do not want to get into a detailed discussion on it, but our whole approach to the problems of agriculture, which hitherto have been tackled piecemeal, was to bring in a national policy to provide for the basic needs of the farmers. First of all we required stability of prices, so we brought in the stabilization act. Then there had to be an attack on the problems of the weather, and we brought in enabling legislation for crop insurance and extended the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Then we had to find new markets, so we started a program of accelerated sales. I could go on and on. This afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was extolling how the Liberal party is the friend of the farmer, and yet when I go to the Bank of Canada report I see on page 33 that farm cash income and

The Budget-Mr. Slogan accrued net farm income has levelled off considerably in growth this year. Surely the farmers of Canada, who this year have done so much for the economy, deserve a better deal from the government.
In our part of the country we have had a severe crop failure this year. I have had a question on the order paper asking what the government intends to do to assist, but it has not been answered, probably because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) is not around. A lot of farmers in our area cannot afford to buy their seed grain this year, and there again the federal government has refused to be of assistance. This is only typical of the Liberal party in its approach to the problems of the nation.
Now a word about devaluation of the dollar. As the former minister of agriculture said, the campaign of the Liberal party on the devaluation of the dollar was the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on the people of Canada because, while the Liberals did not believe that devaluation was not a good thing for Canada, they led the people of Canada to believe it was not. I say that, because if they had believed it was not good they would certainly have done something to restore the premium on the dollar.
But what has devaluation done? Even for the farmer it has meant a 15 cents a bushel increase in price of wheat on world markets. It has increased our competitive position and the position of our exports. I have mentioned what was done with our international balance of payments. For the first time in our history we have a positive balance in our tourist trade, and for this again devaluation of the dollar is largely responsible. It also has meant a decrease of imports into the country, because devaluation has made our domestic products more competitive with the products from low wage countries. To be honest, I think the Minister of Finance and the politicians of the Liberal party should welcome devaluation and should say it was a good thing for Canada; that they have misled the people of Canada and that the policy of the Conservative government at that time was a proper one. I also say that in order to attain the goals we need in our economy, if it is necessary to devaluate the dollar further, then I am in favour of it. Many countries in the world have devaluated their currency. For example, the British pound was $5, and see what it is today. A devaluation of 7J per cent is nothing drastic; it has done a lot of good for the economy, and if further devaluation would do more good, I would be in favour of it.
Now I want to deal with a more noncontroversial subject about which I wish to express some views which perhaps do not


reflect the opinions of other members of the house on either side. As a young man I am not so preoccupied with the past as with the conditions of the present and the prospects for the future. If we are to progress in this country there is room for improvement everywhere. Perhaps we could start right here in this chamber. As members of parliament, we have basic shortcomings. I think we are very pragmatic in our approach to the problems of the country, have an insatiable fear of the electorate and are also very reticent to take a stand on anything but the most non-controversial problems.
I think we are followers rather than leaders in this country. In this day and age, people expect their members of parliament to be leaders. I believe that, as a central government in this country, we must resolve to make the federal government a more effective instrument not only on the home front but amongst the nations of the world. We must inspire amongst Canadians a respect for the government and patriotism in this country, which I think is disintegrating at this time. I believe that, as trustees of Canada, it is our duty to establish unity and opportunity for all Canadians from whatever section of Canada, from whatever racial background or from whatever economic conditions they may come.
It is the duty of the federal government to assist the weak, to restrain the strong, to instil in the average Canadian a greater sense of duty and a greater destiny for Canada. I think we must become partners, too, with all the other levels of government, with all the segments of our economy. This makes for progress and for a modern, enthusiastic society. To a large measure, this philosophy is embodied in the philosophies of the political parties and in the philosophy of the Conservative party which can be described very simply as the vision to create and the courage to retain, and in the words of the motto of our party, which is "opportunity, security and freedom".
If we are going to do something about the problem, it is not enough to just define it. I think we must study the methods which will correct what we lack in our economy today. It is necessary to give vitality to this country, which seems to be lacking, just as we did in 1957 with that vision of the north, the new frontier and the great national development policy we brought into effect. Hon. members should recall that we started the roads to resources program. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said we were building roads from igloo to igloo. I think all members on the other side will regret that phrase. This was reminiscent of the

defeatist Grit opposition in the early days when we were building railways, as they said, from wigwam to wigwam. This is not the type of vision or outlook we want in Canada. We want a vision that is going to bring greater progress to Canada than we have at the moment.
As I said, we could start in the House of Commons itself because I believe that in approaching problems in this house we are often archaic. We are often ineffective. We spend a lot of money and time uselessly. I welcome, therefore, the reconvening of the committee on rules. I only hope that they will have some amendments to bring forth which will make the government more effective without in any way restraining the opposition in their rights to criticize the government.
I feel, too, we need to reconvene a federal-provincial conference with a view to redefining the areas of responsibility under the constitution. We have had the British North America Act for almost 100 years, and it has served us well. But, more and more, we see that there is duplication in government which I believe leads to a waste of money. This duplication has built a government too large to be effective. I think that by redefining the areas of responsibility of the various governments we will be doing a service to Canada. If we can also encourage amongst the provinces something that has been started already, we will be doing a service. I refer to horizontal association, and by that I mean the provinces themselves getting together in those areas of activity which are distinctly the responsibilities of the provinces. The provinces should not have to come to the federal government in connection with responsibilities which are strictly those of the provinces.
These days we hear a lot of talk about co-operative federalism. In those areas where responsibility is shared, I think it is going to be necessary to have closer links with the provinces. Certainly, the record of the former Conservative government in this regard was an admirable one. The principle we have to follow is that the government that is going to spend the money must take the responsibility of levying the taxes. I do not believe demands can be made on the federal treasury all the time unless those who are going to spend the money take the responsibility for levying the taxes. This federal government, during the short time it has been in power, has failed in a lot of respects in relation to its responsibilities with the provinces. I think it has failed and, at the same time, it has weakened the strength of the central government. I do not believe any province
The Budget-Mr. Slogan should hope to establish itself as an equal of the federal government. In the interests of a strong, united Canada, the central government must remain strong and must remain dominant. This has been the policy of the Conservative party since confederation and I think it is still the policy of the Conservative party.
I hope that the Liberal party will not be doing the things it has been doing to create disunity in the country. I want to refer for a moment to the royal commission on bicul-turalism and bilingualism. Since the establishment of this commission I have noticed that in many parts of Canada people who normally had the greatest good will toward the province of Quebec are becoming irritated. A lot of this good will is being lost. I believe these people resent the manner in which the extremists of that province are presenting their problems. In this regard, I feel communications media have a great responsibility. This is one area in which I think they have failed. They have failed the people of Canada, and they have failed their own profession by giving undue attention to that small portion of the population which holds these extreme views and playing them up in the newspapers, on television and radio. I feel the communications media, too, has a responsibility in connection with uniting this country and in connection with building a greater Canada. Statements have been made by people like Rene Levesque and even our present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay). I think when the minister refers to members of this house and the traditions in this house in a way which would exclude some members-and I would be one of them-from positions in the house, he is making the type of statement that does not make for unity and harmony in this country.
I believe a study needs to be made in this area, but certainly a more positive approach could be used than by coining artificial words such as "biculturalism" and "bilingualism" which, by their connotation, spread abroad the idea of the lack of an integral whole. Through the intervening time since confederation, Canadians as a whole have been taught to be tolerant and to respect the views of all. Regardless of their background, they have been taught to be proud of their distinctive contribution to our culture. Terms such as mosaic, flower garden, rainbow and other such apt phrases have been applied to the distinctive blending and fine harmony that has been reached in the Canadian culture. We in the Conservative party are distinctly proud of our promotion of the idea of unhyphenated Canadianism. Canadians today, individually, should be proud enough to assert their status

The Budget-Mr. Slogan as Canadians, without being relegated to first, second or third class Canadians, as much of the publicity surrounding the commission on biculturalism and bilingualism has done inadvertently.
In the few minutes I have left, I want to come back to what I believe the Liberal party can do in order to attain some of these objectives which they have set for themselves and which they have failed to attain. I believe that what we need in Canada is what I would call "A Canada charter-a partnership for progress". This would be a partnership between the federal government and the other levels of government, a partnership between government and the other segments of the economy. First of all, I think it is up to the federal government to be the leader in this respect. It is up to the federal government, if we are to prosper, to relate the segments of economy. It is up to the federal government to define the goals specifically and then plan for their attainment. I believe every effort must be put forward toward recruiting other aspects of our economy in the attainment of these goals.
The minister did mention some of these goals in passing. He referred to increased employment, increased growth, expanded trade and stable prices. There are others such as a sound immigration policy and the guarantee of a minimum standard of living for those of our people who through no fault of their own, are unable to participate as fully as other Canadians do in our prosperity.
Perhaps it would be good for us to look at these goals a little more closely. Basically we are a free enterprise economy and it is our goal to maintain that free enterprise economy because at least in the field of agriculture we can say today that democracy with its freedom is a far superior way of life to that behind the iron curtain. When we consider that the very small proportion of our population in Canada which is engaged in agriculture is producing great surpluses compared with the very large percentage of the population in the Soviet union engaged in agriculture, and failing to produce enough to feed the population of that country, then certainly this is one area where the free enterprise system is more efficient.
I think one of the partnerships we must look to, as well as partnership of the various levels of government, is the partnership of labour, management and government. It is obvious that labour, management and government each has a role to play in attaining these goals. The leader in the attaining of prosperity must be the government, and it is up to us to establish a partnership for progress with each sector of the economy.


In my view we must co-operate with labour to guarantee to the worker a decent minimum wage. I think we must encourage a sound wage structure that will give the worker a decent standard of living. I think we must see that labour is free and responsible in collective bargaining. I think labour must be a partner in increasing efficiency and productivity. In return I think that management too can do something for labour by instituting profit sharing schemes and by making available to their workers equity shares in industry. I think that workers should be proud enough of the company for which they work to invest in it by buying equity shares. In this way they would be investing in the future of their own industry and in Canada as a whole.
At the same time there are responsibilities that labour must accept. Labour must accept the responsibility of not crippling essential industries by irresponsible strikes. There must be freedom for the individual within the labour movement. There must be the largest scope of autonomy for Canadian unions. Unrealistic wage demands that create unstable prices must be avoided. I think that, more than in the past, management and labour must work together, assess their common goals and work harmoniously to achieve them, because only in this way can we achieve a larger share of the world market where our prosperity really lies.
In my view management and industry should be able to look to the government for the proper climate and opportunity for expansion. Management must avoid unsound price advances. Technological advances must be coupled with concern for human displacement. Most of all, industry must be concerned with increasing trade abroad. As one of our ministers said, they had better get off their fannies and sell.
With regard to management and industry, governments must be vigilant to protect displaced workers and to discourage unsound price advances that affect those on fixed incomes and hurt our competitive position abroad. We must be vigilant in our protection and encouragement of small businesses against combines and cartels which eliminate competition.
The government must realize also that following the devastation by war a large portion of European industries has set up new plants, which have become more competitive. Therefore there must be tax incentives for our industries in order that they may improve their plants and place themselves in a competitive position. At a time when European costs are rising, I think that such incentives would do a great deal for Canadian industry.

We in the Conservative party initiated loans to small businesses, a departure from previous years. We expanded export-import insurance. We convened the greatest trade promotion conference in Canadian history. These are some of the things which the Liberal party could emulate.
1 want to refer for a moment to the national debt because actually what we are doing by the vast increase in the national debt is mortgaging future generations of Canadians.
I think the national debt should be of real concern to every Canadian. In an article in the Ottawa Journal I noticed it was estimated that the federal debt went up by $50 for each Canadian in the past year, which is twice the rise of recent years on a per capita basis. The total national debt stands at something like $15,136 million or $789.10 per capita. Perhaps a better way of assessing the impact of the debt on the economy is to realize that in every family with two children the breadwinner is saddled with a mortgage of $3,156.40 and that it is costing the breadwinner of every family with two children $216.44 to pay the carrying charges on the national debt, which this year will amount to $1,038 million. If the government would make the people aware of this fact I think there would certainly be more co-operation with regard to the demand for a balanced budget and a reduction in the national debt to free money that could be invested in the national economy.
In my opinion, continuing deficits will only aggravate the situation. Balancing the budget and reducing the national debt at this time of relative prosperity would do a great deal to free money and make it available for capital investment in the country. I am not saying that deficits are not indicated in certain instances. For example, in a time of recession such as we inherited from the Liberal government, although personal savings in the banks were at an all time high-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member's interesting remarks on the national debt had to be interrupted. If the 1963 budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) could be described as a time bomb which blew up in his face with a loud bang, I think one can only say that the sound that came forth from the present budget was the equivalent of the small plop when a cork is withdrawn from a bottle. While the minister may attempt to describe the contents of the bottle
The Budget-Mr. Barnett to us as vintage champagne, I am afraid that to many of us it tastes more like stale soda water.
However, I really do not wish to concern myself for any length of time with what I would term the superficialities of the budget, but rather I should like to suggest that when a Liberal minister of finance brings down a budget we see Liberal government revealed in its true colours. We see that when it comes to the pinch the Liberal party and the Liberal government always seem to come down firmly on the side of the exploiters and not the exploited. While it may be true that they try to cover up this situation with a few small sops thrown to the people at large, such as the minor extension in family allowances, nevertheless as far as I am concerned this is the basic situation which the budget presented by the amiable Minister of Finance has revealed to us.
I know it is quite true that we who sit here in the House of Commons as members of the New Democratic party often find ourselves giving at least partial approval to many of the proposals which the Liberal government brings forward, proposals, for example, such as the rather fragmentary Canada pension plan or the proposal to send a peace keeping force to Cyprus. However, we in this party are committed to a very different basic point of view so far as the purpose and function of a budget in our government and society are concerned.
I note too from time to time we find ourselves agreeing and quite rightly saying that some of the ministers are doing a good job in administering their departments. I think many of the ministers would agree that we in the N.D.P. are quite prepared to co-operate with them in the proper sense of the term, as members of parliament., in assisting them to do an efficient job of administering the normal affairs of government. But the house, the Minister of Finance and the government should not be misled, by that seeming pleasantry on occasion on our part, into any idea that we find ourselves agreeing in any fundamental way with the government in power.
The occasion of the presentation of the budget is one when we should certainly try to stand up in the house and make ourselves clear on this point. We also find among hon. members opposite, who officially support the government, many nice, well-meaning, idealistic people. They are some of the best examples of do-gooders in our society, and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) who spoke a little earlier, is an excellent example of that sort of person. They are the people who, from time to time, bring modest pressure on the government to introduce

The Budget-Mr. Barnett measures designed to improve public health, to improve the situation of the aged, and to help keep the ill from starving.
They have strong humanitarian impulses, and I freely admit this. We in the New Democratic party share those humanitarian impulses with them; but when budget time comes, and with the customary pomp and ceremony the Minister of Finance stands up to deliver his speech, time after time we find we still have a government that is wedded to the philosophy of the jungle law, where the strong are allowed to eat the weak, and that all the humanitarian impulses of the do-gooders have not got us very far.
To illustrate that point I would like to read a portion of a letter which I received from one of my constituents. It says:
Dear Mr. Barnett:
I may sound very bitter to you but I've reason to be so. Dr. Peterson sees me every two weeks, and he told me he was doing all he could for me, the only thing was new lungs, an operation that can't be done, lungs are gone with bronchitis, some days I can hardly walk with one leg having chronic trouble.
The board in Vancouver turned me down because I can feed myself with a spoon and go to toilet myself.
They are being bribed by someone-
I am not suggesting that I agree with her reasoning, but I can understand her feelings.
-to not give it to me in hopes that by next year I won't need it and will be dead.
There is an example of the kind of situation that I feel very well illustrates the basic position taken by the government of Canada over the years. This woman is partly blind but she is not blind enough to qualify for a blind pension. I know this because I tried my best to get it for her. She is physically disabled but is not disabled enough to qualify for a disabled person's allowance. So she must go along, eking out the barest and most miserable of existences, and I cannot blame her when she comes to the conclusion that boards and governments are just sitting down hoping that before next year she will be dead.
Another example of the fact that in a country as wealthy as Canada we still have a government wedded to the philosophy of the jungle law is the Canada pension plan, which was introduced with such a flourish in this house. As I say, it is something which we in this party will be supporting, but we should not let it go unnoted that as it is proposed it leaves completely unanswered the problems of all the people who will retire during the next ten years in the period the plan is coming into operation. The government will be quite content to let the law of the jungle apply and allow those people to die off in misery and semi-starvation.

Every time the Liberal government unveils a new budget we find the situation remains where the rich will continue to get richer and the poor will continue to get poorer in terms of the productive capacity of the country's economy. I shall not belabour statistics, but anyone who sits down and analyses the figures which are put out in reams by the dominion bureau of statistics can easily see that this is borne out by the facts. Each time a new budget is introduced we find that the ever encroaching monopoly of corporate interests is being encouraged to expand its near dictatorial control over the lives of its wage slaves.
Some hon. members may say that "wage slaves" is a pretty old-hat sort of term which went out with the nineteenth century. Well, Mr. Speaker, any hon. members who really try to understand the problems faced from day to day by the working people, who carry the burden of the sweat and toil, must understand the encircling influences put around them by so many of the employing interests in this country, and will have to agree that the term "wage slaves", far from being old-hat, is becoming more and more true and in a much more insidious fashion than it was in the nineteenth century.
When I use this term I am not referring only to the so-called blue collar workers. I am referring even more to the brains that are hired by these modern corporate dictatorships. I can give one example which happened in my own constituency within the last year.
It concerns a capable office worker for a certain company. He had one son who was a student at the University of British Columbia. This man and his wife displayed some interest in the public affairs of the country, which took the form of general support for my candidacy, and when this happened the powers that be in the company went to the man's wife and told her that if she and her husband did not cease and desist there would be no summer employment for her son, employment which had been promised him. If that sort of thing does not constitute a form of wage slavery, then I really do not know what does. I am sure many high-minded members on the opposite side of the house would agree with me that this is not the sort of thing which should be tolerated; but the question is, what are they prepared to do about it?
Just what does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) do when he enunciates the basic financial and economic policies of the government? These infringements upon civil liberties, these infringements upon the freedom of the mind, these enslavements of Canadian citizens are allowed to go on virtually unchallenged in the name of free enterprise. This is one of the matters on

which members of the New Democratic party And themselves in fundamental disagreement with the government, and with policies and proposals of the kind which are brought forward by the Minister of Finance when he stands up and delivers his budget speech.
Everyone agrees that in a complex industrial society discipline in the productive process is necessary. But we in this party maintain that those who do the controlling and the directing must be responsible for their actions to those who are controlled, if human freedom is to have any meaning, if slavery of the mind and exploitation of the human body and brain are to be brought to an end. This is the state of affairs, however, against which the budgetary policies of the government do not lift even a little finger. Indeed, this particular budget makes it clear that such autocracy is to be continued and even extended.
The budget itself provides one of those occasions when the real difference between those satisfied, well-meaning, do-gooding Liberals and those who subscribe to the social democratic philosophy becomes apparent. The New Democratic party is the only party in Canada which has as a conscious aim the bringing to an end of the exploitation of man by man. We who sit in this house now, and those who will succeed us in the years ahead, will not rest until exploitation has been eliminated from our society. The government and its followers and all the exponents of so-called free enterprise in this country assume that the mainspring of progress must forever be the law of the jungle, with the redness of tooth and claw kept decently out of sight as far as possible. They are content, for the most part, to introduce measures which merely make the fur over the claws a little thicker and a little glossier. Sometimes they even attempt to train the tigers to keep their claws drawn behind the fur. On other occasions they make an attempt to file off the ends of the claws a little so as to blunt them if they do protrude. Then, of course, on occasions, Liberal governments and those who think very much like them, do attempt to add a strand or two to the feeble leashes which are designed to hold the tiger in check; in other words, they bring in such legislation as the combines legislation, the labour laws and the marketing legislation designed to help the farmers. By and large we support these actions because we are humanitarians, too. But let the government know, and let the people of Canada know that we are not satisfied with this sort of thing alone. Specifically, and in direct reference to the budget we are discussing, we disagree completely with the comfortable, complacent "all's well with the world"
The Budget-Mr. Barnett attitude expressed by the minister in his budget speech. Our want of confidence in this government's budget is complete.
Let me make it clear, however, that our want of confidence is not simply a matter of demanding an election this year or next year. We in this party are quite prepared to accept the verdict of the electorate as it is rendered from time to time in general elections. But we do reserve our right to continue to expose the realities of the situation. This budget is really no different from last year's or from that of the year before. It is no different from any budget delivered by a minister of finance in this house in the last 10, 20, 30 or 50 years. All of them have been weighted in favour of the privileged. All of them have encouraged more people in this country to become bloodsucking leeches in our society.
One of the anomalies, I think, of our history is the fact that the only Canadian prime ministers who have shown any signs of radicalism since the first world war have been Conservatives. Mr. R. B. Bennett was going to blast his way into the markets of the world during the depression. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was going to blast unemployment off the map. Neither of them got very far, and this was because neither of them subscribed to a philosophy which could provide them with a reasoned follow through in policy. And, for that matter, neither of them had a parliamentary army which would have followed them had they tried to do that sort of thing.

speechtext:
I hope I have not sounded too wrathful in my denunciation of the hon. gentleman's budget. I must say that if I do feel some wrath it was heightened this year by the failure of the minister to make even the feeblest effort to resolve some of the income tax problems which were discussed last year affecting those who make the greatest effort to provide themselves with income-those who live on salaries and wages. I did have some small hope after the discussion which took place last year that proposals would be made in this year's budget to deal with the grievances which were raised; that there might, indeed, be some proposal to amend section 5 in an appropriate way so as to provide for expenses incurred by those in receipt of wages and salaries. I have been arguing this matter

The Budget-Mr. Pilon in the house since I first came here in 1953, and I suppose if I am here in 1973 and the Minister of Finance is still over there I shall probably still be arguing it. Just for the record I will read one of many letters that I have received on this subject from constituents in recent weeks. This letter is addressed to me, and it says:
I am writing to you, as my elected member of parliament for Comox-Alberni, regarding desired amendments to the Income Tax Act.
Because I am a logger I had to pay out a total of $204.40 in fares last year in getting back and forth to my place of employment. These fares were not paid for holidays but because the operation is closed seasonally. While I was in camp I had to pay board and lodging costs of $536.50. This is a huge sum when you consider that I am at the same time paying $65.00 per month house rent plus additional costs for my own family dwelling elsewhere. Special logging clothes; work boots; hard hat and a rubber rain suit cost me $100 last year.
Please note I have not included cost of regular working clothes which in logging are subject to rapid wear and tear.
As a logging truck driver employed in a logging camp, I not only have the above costs to contend with, but also find that I have an annual cost of $90 replacing broken or worn out tools. I am also finding that every month I am buying some tool to do required maintenance on the new machinery that is coming into my camp. In accepting a job as a truck driver I am required to supply my own tools, so that my fare to camp is increased by $25 every time that my place of employment is changed.
I would like to point out that with recent increases in salaries to M.P.'s, $6,000 was made to be tax free. This money alone is more than I am able to gross each year.
Would you please tell me what steps you have taken or will take during the current session to grant me some relief from this unfair burden.
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the question I would like to direct to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who is in a much better position-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He doesn't care.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-to answer than I am as to what can effectively be done or will effectively be done in this connection. Even if there had been only one little gesture to the people who incur these expenses regularly in the course of earning a fairly modest livelihood, I would have felt a little happier with the budget which the minister has introduced. The only income tax gesture which people such as the man who has written to me are apt to hear much about is that nice little gesture in the minister's proposals to increase to 50 per cent from 30 per cent the annual depreciation allowance on mobile earthmoving equipment. Some of these men will be carting the tools that will be used to repair that equipment from time to time.
So in closing all I can say, in despair of convincing the minister, to those humanitarian members who sit along the back benches

across the way and like to talk so loudly about how they want to see greater justice and how they want to see poverty removed is, "Shame on you. How can you go on supporting a government which brings in the kind of budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance?"
