subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now one of them stands up to confess his shame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the Minister of Finance for presenting a budget which is as realistic as it is practical. This year, the emphasis was put on our young people, those who will be called up to play an important role in the economic structure of our country, that generation which will have to face new obstacles and a more advanced civilization, a more complex economic system and more strained relations within confederation.
Mr. Speaker, the figures and statistics given in the budget reflect a sound and growing economy and also show a new vitality, injected by a Liberal policy conceived by clearsighted and practical businessmen, with the means at our disposal.
The evil of unemployment, in spite of a marked improvement is still an important problem in some eastern sections of the country. It is obvious that in the near future, the steps taken last year and this year will have some beneficial effects. Afterwards, we may enjoy considerably improved conditions and this will greatly contribute to improve our standard of living.
Mr. Speaker, the budget is based on carefully thought out objectives, as mentioned by the minister. Creation of new jobs, steps taken to make sure that the jobs will be filled by well-qualified persons, development and improved economic levels, based on the foresight and ability of our business men, our federal, provincial and municipal authorities.
Our foreign trade has fallen off from 1958 to 1962 and it is essential to regain the share of international markets to which we are entitled. It must be acknowledged that we had been pushed back to the fifth place in that field, whereas in 1957, we were in second place. Every section of our country benefited from this economic recovery. As I said earlier, several factors must be taken into account, more especially our domestic and external markets, our wheat exports, which helped our highway and railway systems, as well as our air transport system. We broke our own records, even in the western provinces where

the recovery was more pronounced thanks to the sustained contribution of our railway systems.
At the outset of my remarks, I said that young people in every part of Canada, those who will eventually replace us later on, will reap the benefits of our legislation. In connection with what I have just said, I should like to emphasize what the late John F. Kennedy said to a group of young people:
What is important, it is not what our country is doing for us, but what we are doing for our country.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I should not like to bore the house by quoting figures and statistics already published and that my honourable colleagues are likely to have seen. I should like now to bring out a point with regard to our constructive legislation.
1.	Assistance will be given to our students by way of income tax relief and family allowances;
2.	The granting of scholarships. The Liberal party platform mentioned the fact that no Canadian would be deprived of an education for financial reasons. I should like also to emphasize the fact that a new department will give leadership to agricultural classes.
Mr. Speaker, may I mention a few facts which will influence the economic outlook of my riding of Chambly-Rouville: the changes with regard to the St. Hubert air station which will be transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Transport.
One of the important industries in my riding had a record year in 1963. The 3 million bushels of apples harvested in the St. Hilaire and Rougemont area were sold quickly and profitably, thanks to new markets, and there was an increase of 30 per cent over the preceding year.
In another field, that of construction, some 800 new home owners, I did say 800, were added to the already long list of those who benefited from C.M.H.C. loans. A piece of legislation passed last year greatly helped the home owners and the building contractors, which reduced unemployment and gave a new impetus to our building materials industry and the sale of lots generally.
I would like to urge both the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the minister responsible for C.M.H.C. to extend the period during which this grant of $500 is allowed, in order that those eligible for it may take advantage of it. The period from November to March is rather short, considering the demand. Our suppliers of materials and C.M.H.C., in spite of every effort, have not been able to cope with the general demand. Statistics show that the building industry has become vitally important during the past
The Budget-Mr. Martineau few years. New building contractors have undertaken colossal projects and have acquired the necessary experience to carry them out. They have put the accent on quality of industrial designs and have helped to revive the building materials trade. They have contributed to improve the standard of our skilled workers and have given Canadians houses worthy of them.
I hope that all right thinking Canadians throughout this country will unite so that Canada will not be broken up. On the other hand, claims from the province of Quebec must not be ignored; that province is ready to co-operate provided its constitutional rights are restored and its identity is preserved.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we shall reach this goal during the year and that we shall give the lie to the extremists' expectations. I believe in a country made up of confederative states, the economy of which is one. We shall find our strength in our differences, having our eyes fixed upon one goal: Canadian unity based upon equal rights.

The Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, has made a pledge, and I want this house to rest assured that we believe in unity and that with the understanding of this great nation this goal will be reached, to the benefit of all Canadians.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a bit late. You will no doubt allow me then to show some kindness. I will start by congratulating the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. He deserves some credit for his speech, but mostly for its brevity.
I also wish to be kind to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon); I know that he deserves it. He must be tired by this debate which has not gone too well for him because I think that very few nice things have been said about his masterpiece, last week's budget.
However, Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the minister is concerned about several groups of citizens. For instance, he worried about the free entry of sacramental bread; that is something in his favour. On the other hand, he recommended the repeal of the provisions concerning the size of whisky bottles. Finally, in order that nobody would be neglected, he amended the tariff on disinfectants, fungicides and insecticides. Consequently, everyone should be satisfied.
One might think that the minister wants to be considered as a humourist. He had already displayed his talent of humourist and actor last year when he was busy pursuing the skeletons which he said were hidden away in the taxation closet. But a year has passed

The Budget-Mr. Martineau and he does not seem to have found any; he took care not to use these terms which he has stricken from his vocabulary since the notorious events which occurred after June 13, 1963.
If I will be permitted to use a well-worn turn of phrase, I would say that the minister turned himself into a mouse this year. So as not to offend him I hasten to say that I am merely making a metaphor; not for a single minute would I think of comparing his physical appearance to that of a mouse. That is not at all what I mean. Considering the apologetic attitude he took when he introduced this production of his, we, on this side of the house, cannot help make such a comparison. Indeed, he pretended to table a budget but he did not quite make it. One would need Diogenes' lantern to find in that document anything that vaguely resembles a budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You mean Theogene.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Diogenes; not Theogene.
I wonder why he was so shy of showing us his masterpiece. Would it be for fear of offending some of his colleagues, those, for instance-we find some on the front benches who want to keep things as they are. Among the most prominent cabinet members, there are some who almost faint every time changes are suggested. However, if there is someone who may be informed about those matters, surely it is the minister, because we know how his most fervent supporters last year made him the target of their criticisms. Maybe he did not want to offend them. Or then again his shyness might have been due to the fact that, this year, he missed the experts who had come from Detroit and Toronto?
This year, the minister has become a supporter of orthodoxy.
He makes a high-sounding statement of policy. Since the budget is a top secret document, according to tradition, he did not deem advisable to call upon outsiders to take part in its preparation. Hurray for the minister. He is beginning to understand. His timidity might be explained by the fact that, even though he looks grave, he is not fully recovered from the shock he suffered last year when he served us that hotchpotch; maybe he tasted it and found it indigestible. Even though he succeeded in swallowing certain items in that budget, certain ingredients of this hotchpotch, it is possible that they are not completely digested.
And while saying this, I am thinking of the tax on building materials and we are still stuck with it. The same applies to his budget especially as he was under the influence of the ides of March, a period of the year which can be full of unexpected phenomenoms and


effects. The minister, scared to death, apologetic and moreover superstitious, even if he says that he is not, presented that masterpiece which I could qualify as a masterpiece of the status quo. And to the house full of anticipation and somewhat apprehensive on account of a past experience, he introduced his freak, this abortive budget. After being an innovator, the minister has become the most eager partisan of the status quo which could be found.
No wonder, therefore, that most hon. members remained dumbfounded at such a display.
On the other hand, I think that the initial surprise and the first moment of amazement having worn off, the inscrutible minister should be asked some questions. Several come to my mind. We could ask the minister why he did not think it appropriate, this year, to abolish his tax on building materials, and production machinery? If he could not abolish it or cancel it altogether, he should at least have prevented it from rising to 8 per cent. Why did he not seize his courage with both hands as he did last year, when as if he had just awakened from a deep slumber, he announced that the full tax would not become effective for some time?
Last year, the minister found as an excuse for this retreat the fact that this tax was "administratively difficult to apply". Therefore, I ask the minister whether this year it became a "administratively easy to apply"? I also ask whether the confusion this tax created in the building field and that of business in general has now completely vanished?
Judging from the briefs from all sections of the country that the minister is still receiving and of which humble hon. members get copies, this confusion still exists, and the builders are still in a state of acute uncertainty because after stocking huge quantities of building materials, etc., in order to avoid the payment of this tax, those people are asking the minister for explanations, but he maintains the same stubborn silence as he did these last few months on that matter.
The minister refuses to see the light and bring the required relief to one of the basic industries of our country, on which depend full employment and the general prosperity of our nation.
At the end of the budget debate, the minister might give us a few answers in this respect.
Now, along other lines, I might ask the minister why he looked after certain special classes of people and why he could not find means to help farmers?
It is true that in reply to a question put to him by some one from this side of the

house, he asked: do they not have any children? Yes, Mr. Speaker, farmers do have children, but they also have particular problems. They are part of one of our country's basic industries. The minister showed a complete lack of interest in the situation of that large segment of our population, whose wheat production especially is now making a substantial contribution towards the solution of one of the problems facing our hon. friends opposite and which he recognizes as the most important, that is the balance of our international payments.
There is nothing in the budget for the farmers; nothing for the worker; nothing for the businessman; and finally no provisions to facilitate property ownership by the people generally. The right of ownership is a basic principle of the Conservative party and it is by favouring ownership that we will be able to preserve our system of free enterprise. The minister did not say one word in this connection. He showed complete indifference, even a hostile attitude towards all those classes of society. I ask him to tell us why?
Why has the budget no provisions to alleviate unemployment? Nevertheless, he is the one who was in favour of full employment in the talks he gave throughout the country, in his programs on television and radio, in his publications and pamphlets, as well as in his famous book. He was supposed to be the one to accomplish this feat of strength.
Today, you can notice his timorous attitude concerning the problem which is at present the most serious one facing the Canadian economy, according to the Prime Minister himself.
At present, there are 400,000 or 500,000 unemployed in Canada. Why is the minister not doing something about it, instead of merely pointing out that the situation is improving? There has been, he said, an improvement.
This improvement is really something fantastic, when one considers the average rate of unemployment, which had risen to 5.9 per cent last year and has now fallen to 5.5 per cent, and this, thanks, as they say-

speechtext: Hear, hear.

-Yes, Mr. Speaker, these gentlemen may well applaud and even smile and make fun of the 400,000 or 500,000 unemployed in this country at this time. But, as I said, if there has been such a microscopic, such a tiny improvement, it is due mainly, as it has been very well recognized, to the dollar devaluation which was, in itself, an initiative that saved Canada. It is also due to the sale of wheat to communist countries, a policy-
The Budget-Mr. Martineau

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those gentlemen's cheers are quite in order, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, a policy launched by those on this side of the house and especially the former minister of agriculture. The Canadian people know what to think about that.
And again, what does the minister intend to do about our balance of payments? Oh, he talks, he makes commendable and pious statements. La Palice himself declared:
We must restore the balance of our payments. We must definitely do it, but what the minister does not say is how we are going to do it. As a matter of fact, he does not give us any indication on this point. He probably thinks that his lucky star, which has for some time shined on high, but which is not as bright at the moment will help him. I have closely examined his budget, but have not found a single solid proposal in it.
What does the minister intend to do, for example, to free this country from public debt charges? In fact, public debt services, for last year and this year, exceed $1 billion. You have there, Mr. Speaker, an astronomical amount, twice as large as the total budget for 1939 and for the sole purpose of paying the interest on the public debt. Nowadays, the federal administration costs twice as much as in 1939.
That is a serious situation which deserves consideration and I am sure the minister is thinking about it. However, he seems to have adopted a do-nothing attitude which is not customary with him and which must surely discourage his best friends.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to know also what the minister intends to do concerning the control of our industry and our business by foreigners. Has he abandoned his aim which was to increase Canadian participation in our industry? Of course, we must not forget that he launched his policy rather clumsily last year when he hastily introduced half-baked measures that he withdrew just as fast. He is quite clear when he defines the objectives we must strive to reach, but when it comes to suggest means of doing so, his statements are most obscure.
He speaks of fiscal measures to achieve these objectives, but then he withdraws the withholding tax on dividends paid to nonresidents. Concerning the withdrawal of this tax, however difficult this action was for the minister, we must congratulate him for it, and we fully agree with him, because last year, one member after the other called for the withdrawal of this discriminatory tax which did not meet the purpose it was meant to. On the contrary.
But we cannot follow the argument of the minister when he gives his excuse for the

The Budget-Mr. Martineau withdrawal of this tax. He mentions vaguely the fact that taxes have been lowered in the United States. He speaks also of the American parent corporations which will pay only 48 per cent tax on their income in 1965, which is the equivalent of a 15 per cent withholding tax.
Mr. Speaker, if you have lost the thread of my argument, I do not blame you. It is precisely the point that I would like to make. You cannot understand me because I am using the very same words used by the Minister of Finance. That is why you do not follow my argument, and I wonder what he is talking about when he gives the reason or rather the excuse that this is a new factor, which is not true, since this concerns the corporate tax cut in the United States. As a matter of fact, it is not new because last year, or more precisely last June 13, when the minister brought down his budget, the U.S. senate had been asked to approve tax cuts. And I would like the minister to give us suitable explanations in that connection.
Mr. Speaker, there are several other questions which remained unanswered. And, in order to be objective, I must also direct other questions to the minister.
Why did he fail to take necessary steps in order to cut government expenditures? Why did he not see fit to cut taxes? And finally, why does he announce, for the fiscal year 1964-65, a deficit of nearly half a billion dollars?
Let us start by considering the matter of deficits. At the outset of his budget speech, the minister said that the economic climate had never been better. He saw everything through pink glasses and said that business was doing better and better.
In the past, the minister used to say that deficits could not be used except when the economy was slowing down. As a matter of fact, it is the theory of the pump primer. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) knows what is meant by the theory of the pump primer.
The minister said that we were entering upon an unprecedented era of prosperity. And yet, he predicted a deficit of half a
billion dollars. If the minister is unable to balance the budget when, according to him, we are living in an unprecedented era of prosperity, I wonder how he will ever manage to balance it. If the minister is the least consistent and logical-I know he is, but then he must have the courage to show it in his actions-in short, if his premises are sound, he should have introduced a balanced budget this year. Otherwise, his basic argument crumbles and the Canadian people can have no faith in his theories, because one cannot look at the dark and the bright side of everything at the same time. And yet, what the minister does not say is that he sees mostly red on account of a $500 million deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make concerning tax cuts. We emphatically demand tax cuts. We, on this side of the house, are supporters of fiscal responsibility, and that is why we are asking for a relief in taxation. We know that taxation relief means renewed activity and an incentive for the whole economy, a stimulus for private enterprise, from which results a larger basis for taxation.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?
